17592186069224 :question/problem "Simplify $\sqrt{32{y}^{3}}$ given that $y\ge 0.$" :question/worked-solution "We first write $32{y}^{3}$ as the product $16{y}^{2}\cdot 2y$ which contains a perfect square $(16{y}^{2}).$ Then, we separate the product into two separate radicals, one of which can be simplified:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{32{y}^{3}} & = \\ \sqrt{16{y}^{2}\cdot 2y} & = \\ \sqrt{(4y)^{2}\cdot 2y} & = \\ \sqrt{(4y)^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{2y} & = \\ |4y|\cdot \sqrt{2y} & = \\ |4|\cdot |y|\cdot \sqrt{2y} & = \\ 4\cdot |y|\cdot \sqrt{2y}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $y\ge 0,$ we have $|y|=y,$ and we can simplify further. Therefore, our final answer is

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot |y|\cdot \sqrt{2y} & = \\ 4\cdot y\cdot \sqrt{2y} & = \\ 4y\sqrt{2y}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186066522 :answer-field/correct 17592186066526 :answer-field/choices ["answer-effe64da-d5ba-51cb-959c-be6a879f598d"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-effe64da-d5ba-51cb-959c-be6a879f598d" :answer/id #uuid "effe64da-d5ba-51cb-959c-be6a879f598d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2{y}^{2}\sqrt{8y}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069943 :tutorial/content "The **product rule for radicals** states that the square root of a product equals the product of the square roots:

$$
\eqalign{
		\sqrt{ab} &=\sqrt{a} \cdot \sqrt{b}
	}
$$

We can use the product rule to rewrite the square roots of algebraic expressions.

As an example, let's suppose we want to simplify the following expression:

$$
\sqrt{32y}
$$

First, we rewrite $32y$ as the product $16 \cdot 2y,$ which contains a perfect square $(16){:}$ 

$$
\eqalign{
	\sqrt{32y}&=\[5pt]
	\sqrt{16 \cdot 2y}&=\[5pt]
	\sqrt{4^2 \cdot 2y}&

	}
$$

Then, we separate the product into two separate radicals using the product rule:

$$
\eqalign{
        \sqrt{4^2\cdot 2y}&=\[3pt]
        \sqrt{4^2}\cdot \sqrt{2y}&
	}
$$

Finally, we simplify the radical containing the perfect square:

$$
\eqalign{
        \sqrt{4^2}\cdot \sqrt{2y}&=\[3pt]
        |4|\cdot \sqrt{2y}&=\[3pt]

	4\sqrt{2y}&
	}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068936 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186133278 :answer-field/choices 17592186133283] [:db/retract 17592186133278 :answer-field/choices 17592186133279] {:db/id 17592186133728 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-770dc96c-77d3-556b-b303-18d387043365"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-770dc96c-77d3-556b-b303-18d387043365" :question/id #uuid "770dc96c-77d3-556b-b303-18d387043365" :question/math-academy-id "q-89606" :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{75}x,\, & 5\le x\le 10 \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

its cumulative distribution function is 

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0,\, & x<5 \\ h(x),\, & 5\le x\le 10 \\ 1,\, & x>10.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the function $h(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Since our random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that is strictly positive only for $5\le x\le 10,$ the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<5 \\ {\int }_{5}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t, & 5\le x\le 10 \\ 1, & x>10\end{aligned}
$$

For the given probability density function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{5}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{5}^{x}\frac{2}{75}t\,\text{d}t \\ \text{ } & ={\frac{1}{75}{t}^{2}|}_{5}^{x} \\  & =\frac{1}{75}{x}^{2}-\frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}-25}{75}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0,\, & x<5, \\ \frac{{x}^{2}-25}{75},\, & 5\le x\le 10, \\ 1,\, & x>10.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-94adf626-a400-5181-b287-7ccffcedb8aa"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-94adf626-a400-5181-b287-7ccffcedb8aa" :answer-field/id #uuid "94adf626-a400-5181-b287-7ccffcedb8aa" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-49f3c406-0b5e-5522-a240-414ac7e0f856" :answer-field/choices ["answer-b55dc857-62d1-5ed0-85ee-8b7c291b0260" "answer-f364853a-396b-5d86-bdbe-5ffe621626d8" "answer-1c522a9a-a340-5730-935a-e853421c44ca" "answer-887364d0-5dcf-5d1a-9cb5-af1322ef590e" "answer-49f3c406-0b5e-5522-a240-414ac7e0f856"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b55dc857-62d1-5ed0-85ee-8b7c291b0260" :answer/id #uuid "b55dc857-62d1-5ed0-85ee-8b7c291b0260" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{75}x" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f364853a-396b-5d86-bdbe-5ffe621626d8" :answer/id #uuid "f364853a-396b-5d86-bdbe-5ffe621626d8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{75}{x}^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1c522a9a-a340-5730-935a-e853421c44ca" :answer/id #uuid "1c522a9a-a340-5730-935a-e853421c44ca" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{75-2x}{75}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-887364d0-5dcf-5d1a-9cb5-af1322ef590e" :answer/id #uuid "887364d0-5dcf-5d1a-9cb5-af1322ef590e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{75-{x}^{2}}{75}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-49f3c406-0b5e-5522-a240-414ac7e0f856" :answer/id #uuid "49f3c406-0b5e-5522-a240-414ac7e0f856" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{{x}^{2}-25}{75}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186134540 :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X$ has the cumulative distribution function

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<0 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{25}, & 0\le x\le 5 \\ 1, & x>5,\end{aligned}
$$

find $P(1\le X\le 3).$" :question/worked-solution "Remember that for continuous random variables, it doesn't matter whether or not we include the endpoints of the interval. So we can perform the computation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(1\le X\le 3) & =P(1<X\le 3) \\  & =P(X\le 3)-P(X\le 1) \\  & =F(3)-F(1) \\  & =\frac{{3}^{2}}{25}-\frac{{1}^{2}}{25} \\  & =\frac{8}{25}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133278 :answer-field/correct 17592186133281 :answer-field/choices ["answer-c3226fc1-cbce-5f81-a7bd-59cad1dcc127" "answer-4a3624d2-d1b2-5d89-8864-4bd4b45113e1"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c3226fc1-cbce-5f81-a7bd-59cad1dcc127" :answer/id #uuid "c3226fc1-cbce-5f81-a7bd-59cad1dcc127" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1+\frac{8}{25}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4a3624d2-d1b2-5d89-8864-4bd4b45113e1" :answer/id #uuid "4a3624d2-d1b2-5d89-8864-4bd4b45113e1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1-\frac{8}{25}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133727 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-b31007d2-c9e1-51d3-8e66-44402735c224" "question-d0e0e171-2942-5666-9f4c-984a9e7d868a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-b31007d2-c9e1-51d3-8e66-44402735c224" :question/id #uuid "b31007d2-c9e1-51d3-8e66-44402735c224" :question/math-academy-id "q-89634" :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$

find the cumulative distribution function $F(x).$" :question/worked-solution "The cumulative distribution function of a continuous random variable $X$ is the function $F(x)$ defined by

$$

$$

For the given probability density function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{3{t}^{2}}{\pi (1+{t}^{6})}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\frac{\operatorname{arctan}⁡({t}^{3})}{\pi }|}_{-\infty }^{x} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{arctan}⁡({x}^{3})}{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}

"d0e0e171-2942-5666-9f4c-984a9e7d868a" :question/math-academy-id "q-185531" :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)=\frac{{e}^{-|x|}}{2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

its cumulative distribution function is

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}^{x}}{2},\, & x\le 0 \\ h(x),\, & x>0\end{aligned}
$$

where $h(x)=${{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "Since our random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that involves an absolute value, the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\{\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{t}}{2}\,\text{d}t, & x<0 \\ {\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t}}{2}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t}}{2}\,\text{d}t, & x\ge 0\end{aligned}
$$

Let's compute the integrals.

- If $x\le 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{t}}{2}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{t}}{2}|}_{-\infty }^{x} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{x}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t}}{2}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{x}}{2}|}_{x=0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t}}{2}\,\text{d}t & =-{\frac{{e}^{-t}}{2}|}_{0}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t}}{2}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t}}{2}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}+(-\frac{{e}^{-x}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =1-\frac{{e}^{-x}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}^{x}}{2},\, & x\le 0 \\ 1-\frac{{e}^{-x}}{2},\, & x>0.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-bb588555-9fd1-5660-8555-bc1960f97262"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "5f7aceb3-5a6a-584b-8488-47f8fb82e9a0" :question/math-academy-id "q-125649" :question/problem "![](images/0f/0f178c33254644c5e2e7bf6f3c596df87b1ea2f0b5bfd417c3f279f6c62b1b0d.png)

Consider the circle $S$ and the vector field $F,$ shown above. Let $C$ be any path where $S$ is traversed once in the **clockwise** direction. Which of the following statements are true?

I. ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$

II. ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0$

III. ${∮}_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$" :question/worked-solution "The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

We now recall the following:

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is false, while statement II is true. It's clear from the picture below that $F$ works against the motion of the particle as it moves clockwise along $C.$ 

![](images/f8/f87d2e735ad58e0b33a813fb91ab202ac0eeaf90575979ea45f954fb7e1d0493.png)

So, $Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

- Statement III is true. It's clear from the picture below that $F$ assists the motion of the particle as it moves counterclockwise along $C.$

![](images/10/102c11f9002e29a3759679c6ff0bd10188908d33eb9cc94a84d900956adc33a5.png)

So, $Γ={∮}_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0bb54f63-1362-5d2e-8c6a-5e8e2485a25f"] :db/ensure "question-2343ccc6-302e-57d1-903e-91d537e6ff5c" :question/id #uuid "2343ccc6-302e-57d1-903e-91d537e6ff5c" :question/math-academy-id "q-161385" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v),$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=⟨-2x,\,-2y,\,-z⟩,\,r(u,v)=⟨{u}^{3},\,{v}^{3},\,uv⟩,\,(u,v)\in D⊂{R}^{2}.
$$

If the flux of $F$ across $S$ with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A
$$

what is the missing expression?

*Hint: You can use the fact that ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}=⟨-3{v}^{3},\,-3{u}^{3},\,9{u}^{2}{v}^{2}⟩.$*" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Notice we are told that the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}=⟨-3{v}^{3},\,-3{u}^{3},\,9{u}^{2}{v}^{2}⟩.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨-2x,\,-2y,\,-z⟩{|}_{x={u}^{3}\,y={v}^{3}\,z=uv} \\  & =⟨-2{u}^{3},\,-2{v}^{3},\,-uv⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨-2{u}^{3},\,-2{v}^{3},\,-uv⟩\cdot ⟨-3{v}^{3},\,-3{u}^{3},\,9{u}^{2}{v}^{2}⟩ \\  & =(-2{u}^{3})\cdot (-3{v}^{3})+(-2{v}^{3})\cdot (-3{u}^{3})+(-uv)\cdot 9{u}^{2}{v}^{2} \\  & =6{u}^{3}{v}^{3}+6{u}^{3}{v}^{3}-9{u}^{3}{v}^{3} \\  & =3{u}^{3}{v}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,3{u}^{3}{v}^{3}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-3fefe9c8-5fc6-5bbb-bfe2-94890c45b24c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Find the moment of the rod about the origin." :question/worked-solution "The moment about the origin $O$ of a rod with mass density function $\lambda (x)$ for $a\le x\le b$ is given by 

$$
{M}_{O}={\int }_{a}^{b}x\,\lambda (x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\lambda (x)=5\sqrt{x},\,a=0,\,b=1.
$$

We calculate the moment of the rod about the origin as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{O} & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\cdot 5\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}5{x}^{3/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[2{x}^{5/2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2\cdot {1}^{5/2}-0 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

$Y$ be two continuous random variables with the following joint probability density function:

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}1, & \,0<x<1,\,x-1<y<1-x \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Find the expression of the conditional probability density function ${f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)$ for $0<x<1,\,x-1<y<1-x.$" :question/worked-solution "Using the formula for the marginal density function for $X,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{x-1}^{1-x}1\,\text{d}y \\  & =y\,{|}_{x-1}^{1-x} \\  & =(1-x)-(x-1) \\  & =2-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the full expression for ${f}_{X}(x)$ is the following:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}2-2x, & \,0<x<1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Now recall that the conditional probability density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ for two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)},
$$

where

- $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability density function for $X$ and $Y,$ and

- ${f}_{X}(x)$ is the marginal density function for $X.$

Now, for $0<x<1,\,x-1<y<1-x,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{1}{2-2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

For other values of $x$ and $y,$ the function $f(x,y)$ equals $0.$ As a result, ${f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)$ will be equal to $0$ too.

Therefore, the conditional probability density function is the following:

$$
{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2-2x}, & \,0<x<1,\,x-1<y<1-x \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186159542 :answer-field/correct "answer-f4fc661d-e145-5e66-b9b9-6631ae091f43" :answer-field/choices ["answer-c42b7b33-0490-5c36-8f01-54cc20ab39d5" "answer-70d54670-c738-50bc-afb0-0d6374b4b4d7" "answer-61b79666-a6d5-539f-81d1-2e3b56449d2b" "answer-f4fc661d-e145-5e66-b9b9-6631ae091f43"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c42b7b33-0490-5c36-8f01-54cc20ab39d5" :answer/id #uuid "c42b7b33-0490-5c36-8f01-54cc20ab39d5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2{x}^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-70d54670-c738-50bc-afb0-0d6374b4b4d7" :answer/id #uuid "70d54670-c738-50bc-afb0-0d6374b4b4d7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{1+x}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-61b79666-a6d5-539f-81d1-2e3b56449d2b" :answer/id #uuid "61b79666-a6d5-539f-81d1-2e3b56449d2b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{1-x}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f4fc661d-e145-5e66-b9b9-6631ae091f43" :answer/id #uuid "f4fc661d-e145-5e66-b9b9-6631ae091f43" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{2-2x}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186172650 :question/problem "A particle moves along a circular path centered at $O$ in the $xy$-plane in the counterclockwise direction with a constant angular velocity of $2\text{ rad/s}.$ Given that the object is at the position $(5,0)$ when $t=0,$ find the position function of the particle." :question/worked-solution "The position function of a particle moving in a circular path of radius $R$ in the $xy$-plane with a constant angular velocity $\omega $ is given by

$$

the variable exponent by dividing both sides by $3$:

$$
\begin{aligned}3\cdot {2}^{y} & =24 \\ \frac{3\cdot {2}^{y}}{3} & =\frac{24}{3} \\ {2}^{y} & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we rewrite $8$ as ${2}^{3}$ to get:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{y} & =8 \\ {2}^{y} & ={2}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since both sides of the equation share the same base $(2)$, we equate the exponents:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{y} & ={2}^{3} \\ y & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $y=3.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8ea04aaa-60fe-5164-9b6a-5f1f5daacdc8"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} "⟨\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡s,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡s,16\operatorname{cos}⁡4s⟩" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199449 :tutorial/content "We can differentiate vector-valued functions with three components in the same way. 

For example, if 

$$
\mathbf{f}(t) = \big\langle x(t), \: y(t), \: z(t) \big\rangle
$$

is our vector-valued function, then the derivative is computed as follows:

$$
\dfrac{ \text{d}\mathbf{f}}{\text{d}t} = \left\langle \dfrac{ \text{d}x}{\text{d}t}, \: \dfrac{ \text{d}y}{\text{d}t}, \: \dfrac{ \text{d}z}{\text{d}t} \right\rangle
$$

 

For example, suppose that we are given the vector function 

$$
\mathbf f (t) = \left\langle t^3, \:  \ln(t+3), \:  \sqrt{t}\right\rangle.
$$

 

To compute the derivative $\mathbf f'\!(t),$ we find the derivative of each component function, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{d}{dt}⟨{t}^{3},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+3),\,\sqrt{t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{d}{dt}({t}^{3}),\,\frac{d}{dt}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+3)),\,\frac{d}{dt}(\sqrt{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2},\,\frac{1}{t+3},\,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198483 :activity/expected-seconds 960.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186171555 :answer-field/choices 17592186171556] [:db/retract 17592186171555 :answer-field/choices 17592186171557] [:db/retract 17592186171555 :answer-field/choices 17592186171558] [:db/retract 17592186171555 :answer-field/choices 17592186171559] [:db/retract 17592186171555 :answer-field/choices 17592186171560] {:db/id 17592186172044 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-5b5c204f-7839-5ec6-95c0-a9151439158a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186172655 :question/problem "A particle moves along a **clockwise** circular path with center $O$ in the $xy$-plane with a constant angular velocity of $2\pi \text{ rad/s}.$ Given that the object is at the position $(3,0)$ when $t=0,$ find the position function of the particle." :question/worked-solution "The position function of a particle moving in a circular path of radius $R$ in the $xy$-plane with a constant angular velocity $\omega $ is given by

$$
r(t)=R(\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t\,j),
$$

where it is assumed that the circle is centered at $O,$ and particle is at the position $(R,0)$ when $t=0.$

Since the object's initial position is $(3,0),$ we have that $r(0)=\,3i,$ and we can conclude that the radius of the circle $R=3.$

Therefore, since we have $R=3$ and $\omega =-2\pi \text{ rad/s}$ (negative because the motion is clockwise), we get that the position function is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =3(\operatorname{cos}⁡(-2\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(-2\pi t)\,j) \\  & =3(\operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi t\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi t\,j).\end{aligned}

Find the magnitude of the acceleration of the object at time $t,$ measured in seconds." :question/worked-solution "**Method 1**

First, we find the velocity vector by differentiating the position vector. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =(r(t))^{′} \\  & =(3(\operatorname{cos}⁡3t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡3t\,j))^{′} \\  & =-9\operatorname{sin}⁡3t\,i+9\operatorname{cos}⁡3t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we find the acceleration vector by differentiating the velocity vector. 

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =(v(t))^{′} \\  & =(-9\operatorname{sin}⁡3t\,i+9\operatorname{cos}⁡3t\,j)^{′} \\  & =-27\operatorname{cos}⁡3t\,i-27\operatorname{sin}⁡3t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the magnitude of the acceleration as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}||a(t)|| & =\sqrt{(-27\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)^{2}+(-27\operatorname{sin}⁡3t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{27}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡3t+{27}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡3t} \\  & =\sqrt{{27}^{2}} \\  & =27\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the magnitude of the acceleration is $27\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$

Note that $||a||$ is constant, but $a$ is not. 

**Method 2**

For uniform circular motion in the $xy$-plane, we have

$$
a=-{\omega }^{2}r\,⇒\,||a||={\omega }^{2}||r||.
$$

In our case, the radius of the circle is $a=3\,\text{m}$ and the angular frequency $\omega =3\,\text{rad/s}.$ Therefore,

$$

If the team lost $9$ games last year, how many games did the team win?" :question/worked-solution "We need to know the total number of games played to determine the number of games won. 

We're given a part and a percentage, and we need to find the whole.

In this case, the part is the number of games the team lost, which is $9.$ The percentage is $18%,$ and the whole is the total number of games played. 

To find the whole, we can use the following formula:

$$
\text{whole}=\text{part}÷\text{percentage}
$$

Before we can substitute our numbers into the formula, we need to express $18%$ as a fraction:

$$
\frac{18}{100}=\frac{18÷2}{100÷2}=\frac{9}{50}
$$

We can now substitute our numbers into the formula, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{whole} & =9÷18% \\  & =9÷\frac{9}{50} \\  & =9\times \frac{50}{9} \\  & =\frac{9}{9}\times 50 \\  & =50\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the total number of games played by the softball team last year was $50.$ The total number of games won is

$$
50-9=41.
$$

Hence, the softball team won $41$ games last year." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0e4089d0-6e83-5bb9-a01d-10713a8e31b3"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-0e4089d0-6e83-5bb9-a01d-10713a8e31b3" :answer-field/id #uuid "0e4089d0-6e83-5bb9-a01d-10713a8e31b3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-0ae02206-f280-552b-9c7e-f1b25280fec4" :answer-field/choices ["answer-bc1ca7bf-82a2-5e5e-8c98-5cf6337f7731" "answer-0ae02206-f280-552b-9c7e-f1b25280fec4" "answer-ae3f93d0-753a-5489-8c3f-af8fc22cc58c" "answer-0bc1090e-61d0-5086-8900-d3ac3d3c7142" "answer-175774cc-bfba-5313-9d4b-4d00fbc5ce0e"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-bc1ca7bf-82a2-5e5e-8c98-5cf6337f7731" :answer/id #uuid "bc1ca7bf-82a2-5e5e-8c98-5cf6337f7731" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "21" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0ae02206-f280-552b-9c7e-f1b25280fec4" :answer/id #uuid "0ae02206-f280-552b-9c7e-f1b25280fec4" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "41" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ae3f93d0-753a-5489-8c3f-af8fc22cc58c" :answer/id #uuid "ae3f93d0-753a-5489-8c3f-af8fc22cc58c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "45" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0bc1090e-61d0-5086-8900-d3ac3d3c7142" :answer/id #uuid "0bc1090e-61d0-5086-8900-d3ac3d3c7142" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "51" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-175774cc-bfba-5313-9d4b-4d00fbc5ce0e" :answer/id #uuid "175774cc-bfba-5313-9d4b-4d00fbc5ce0e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "61" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186148781 :tutorial/content "To find a part given a percent and whole, we can use the following formula:

$$
\textrm{percent} \times \textrm{whole} = \textrm{part}
$$

However, we sometimes want to find a whole given a part and a percent. To do this, we can use the relationship between multiplication and division to rewrite the above formula as follows:

$$
\textrm{whole} = \textrm{part} \div \textrm{percent}
$$

Let's use this formula to find the missing number in the following statement:
![](images/08/082c6ac53fa8de85b739dde0611943e92cb09d74d07378d6a33043d4b231e88d.svg)

In this case, the part is $540$, and the percent is $30\%.$ 

We can express $30\%$ as a fraction as follows:

$$
\dfrac{30}{100} = \dfrac{30\div 10}{100\div 10} = \dfrac{3}{10}
$$

Putting these numbers into our formula for the whole, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{whole} & =\text{part}÷\text{percent} \\  & =540÷30% \\  & =540÷\frac{3}{10} \\  & =540\times \frac{10}{3} \\  & =\frac{540}{3}\times 10 \\  & =180\times 10 \\  & =1,800\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the missing number is $1,800.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186147657 :activity/expected-seconds 480.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179681 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-cb6a3551-b7c8-5448-9dd7-361a94a204ac" "question-a4309379-1166-58a1-b1ee-b77ecf90fd3f"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179540 :question/problem "Find the real solution to the equation $96x^5=3.$" :question/worked-solution "We can solve this equation by isolating the $x^5$ term and then taking the $5$th root of each side.

First, let's isolate the $x^5$ term on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}96{x}^{5} & =3 \\ {x}^{5} & =\frac{1}{32}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we take the $5$th root of each side and solve for $x.$ Since $n=5$ is odd, there is only one real solution to this equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{5} & =\frac{1}{32} \\ \sqrt[5]{{x}^{5}} & =\sqrt[5]{\frac{1}{32}} \\ x & =\sqrt[5]{{(\frac{1}{2})}^{5}} \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=\dfrac12.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179680 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-ea193efd-d8e8-59fc-adc1-1d1595da20e0" "question-e173cb82-cae9-5da1-9ec4-a1b561689a6a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179539 :question/problem "Find the real solution to the equation $5(x-6)^7 = 640.$" :question/worked-solution "We can solve this equation by isolating the $(x-6)^7$ term and then taking the $7$th root of each side.

First, let's isolate the $(x-6)^7$ term on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}5(x-6)^{7} & =640 \\ (x-6)^{7} & =128\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we take the $7$th root of each side and solve for $x.$ Since $n=7$ is odd, there is only one real solution to this equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-6)^{7} & =128 \\ \sqrt[7]{(x-6)^{7}} & =\sqrt[7]{128} \\ x-6 & =\sqrt[7]{{2}^{7}} \\ x-6 & =2 \\ x & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=8.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-cb6a3551-b7c8-5448-9dd7-361a94a204ac" :question/id #uuid "cb6a3551-b7c8-5448-9dd7-361a94a204ac" :question/math-academy-id "q-111446" :question/problem "Find the real solution to the equation ${x}^{3}=-512.$" :question/worked-solution "We can solve this equation by taking the $3$rd root of each side and solving for $x.$ Since $n=3$ is odd, there is only one real solution to this equation:

$$
x^3 = 125?
$$

We can solve this equation by taking the $3$rd root of each side and solving for $x.$ 

Since $n=3$ is odd, there will be only one real solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3} & =125 \\ \sqrt[3]{{x}^{3}} & =\sqrt[3]{125} \\ x & =\sqrt[3]{{5}^{3}} \\ x & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=5.$

In general, we have the following rule of thumb:

*When $n$ is odd, and we take the $n$th root of both sides of $x^n = a,$ we get only one solution:* 

$$
x = \sqrt[n]{a}

$$
5\sqrt{x} - 3\sqrt{x}
$$

We can simplify our expression by combining the two radicals, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}5\sqrt{x}-3\sqrt{x} & = \\ (5-3)\sqrt{x} & = \\ 2\sqrt{x} & \end{aligned}
$$

We *cannot* combine terms when the expressions under the radical are different. For example, the expression

$$
5\sqrt{x} - 3\sqrt{y}
$$

cannot be simplified because there is no way of combining $\sqrt x$ and $\sqrt y.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186180750 :tutorial/content "We can simplify cube root expressions in the same way as with square roots.

$$

$$
{{z}^{2}+2\cdot 7z+{7}^{2}}_{⏟}-{7}^{2}+19
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
(z+7)^{2}-{7}^{2}+19
$$

$$
(z+7)^{2}-30
$$

$$

$$

$$

First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with $2$ as a factor:

$$
{y}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{5}y-\frac{4}{25}
$$

Then, we *add* and *then subtract* ${(\frac{1}{5})}^{2},$ writing the constant term $\frac{4}{25}$ last:

$$
{{y}^{2}-2\cdot \frac{1}{5}y+{(\frac{1}{5})}^{2}}_{⏟}-{(\frac{1}{5})}^{2}-\frac{4}{25}
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
{(y-\frac{1}{5})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{5})}^{2}-\frac{4}{25}
$$

Evaluating the last two terms, we get

$$
{(y-\frac{1}{5})}^{2}-\frac{1}{5}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}-5({y}^{2}-\frac{2}{5}y-\frac{4}{25}) & =-5({(y-\frac{1}{5})}^{2}-\frac{1}{5}) \\  & =-5{(y-\frac{1}{5})}^{2}+(-5)\cdot (-\frac{1}{5}) \\  & =-5{(y-\frac{1}{5})}^{2}+1\end{aligned}

- The *square of the shortest distance from $P(x,y)$ to the $x$-axis* is given by ${y}^{2}.$

$$
{y}^{′}=k\cdot {y}^{2},
$$

where $k$ is a constant.

So, our differential equation is

$$
{y}^{′}=k{y}^{2}.

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=k{r}^{2}
$$

where $k>0.$

We wish to use this information to find an expression for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$

The area of a circle is given by 

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}.
$$

 

Differentiating this equation with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =2\pi r\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=k{r}^{2} \\ 2\pi r\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=k{r}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=\frac{k{r}^{2}}{2\pi r} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=\frac{kr}{2\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

We now introduce a new constant:

$$
K=\frac{k}{2\pi }>0
$$

 

Therefore, our equation becomes

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=Kr.

[:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186189375 :tutorial/content "When constructing a differential equation to model a particular phenomenon, we sometimes combine several pieces of information to create the correct model.

Consider the following situation:

*The common cold virus spreads through a particular country. The rate at which the number of infected people increases is **proportional** to the **square of the time** $t$ (in days) since the outbreak started. 
Additionally, $100$ infected people **recover from the virus each day**.*

We want to find a differential equation that models $P(t),$ the number of infected people. We note the following:

- The statement describes the *rate* at which the *number of infected people* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d P}{\textrm d t}.
$$

- The rate at which the number of infected people increases is **proportional** to the **square of the time** $t.$ Therefore, if $I(t)$ represents the rate at which infections increase, then

$$
I(t) = kt^2,
$$

where $k$ is a positive constant.

- Additionally, $100$ infected people **recover from the virus each day**. Therefore, if $D(t)$ represents the rate at which infections decrease, then

$$
D(t) = 100.
$$

Therefore, the differential equation that describes this phenomenon is as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}P}{\text{d}t} & ={{k{t}^{2}-100}_{⏟}}_{I(t)-D(t)}\end{aligned}
$$

Although we introduced the functions $I(t)$ and $D(t)$ here, we can usually write down the appropriate differential equation straight away. Let's see an example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186189439 :tutorial/content "Let's recall some basic facts from geometry in the $xy$-plane:

- The distance between the point $(x,y)$ and the origin $(0,0)$ equals $\sqrt{x^2+y^2}.$

- The (smallest) distance between the point $(x,y)$ and the $x$-axis equals $|y|.$

- Similarly, the (smallest) distance between the point $(x,y)$ and the $y$-axis equals $|x|.$

- The slope of the line that passes through $(x,y)$ and the origin equals $\dfrac{y}{x}.$

We sometimes need to use these basic facts when constructing differential equations described in a geometric context.

To construct the point-slope form of the line, we need a point and a slope. We already have two points, so we calculate the slope $m$ using the given points:

$$
\begin{aligned}m=\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}}=\frac{7-0}{4-0}=\frac{7}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use this slope along with one of the points to write the point-slope form equation of the line. It doesn't matter which point we choose, but let's choose $(0,0).$ The point-slope equation is as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-0 & =\frac{7}{4}(x-0) \\ y & =\frac{7}{4}x\end{aligned}
$$

To simplify the point-slope formula into standard form, we first multiply by $4$ to get rid of the fraction:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{7}{4}(x) \\ 4\cdot (y) & =4\cdot \frac{7}{4}(x) \\ 4y & =7x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we move the variables to the left side and the constant to the right side:

$$
\begin{aligned}4y & =7x \\ -7x+4y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we multiply by $-1$ to make the $x$-coefficient positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}-7x+4y & =0 \\ (-1)\cdot (-7x+4y) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 7x-4y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$

eigenvalue $\lambda =\pi ,$ a generalized eigenvector of rank $3$ is a vector $v$ such that 

$$
(B-\pi I)^{3}v=0\,\text{and}\,(B-\pi I)^{2}v\ne 0.
$$

Notice the following:

- We are given that $\text{Null}(B-\pi I)^{2}$ has dimension $2.$ This means that the solutions to $(B-\pi I)^{2}v=0$ form a subspace of dimension $2.$

- We are given that $\text{Null}(B-\pi I)^{3}$ has dimension $3.$ This means that the solutions to $(B-\pi I)^{3}v=0$ form a subspace of dimension $3.$

Now, since $\text{Null}(B-\pi I)^{2}$ is a subspace of dimension $2$ in $\text{Null}(B-\pi I)^{3}$, which is a subspace of dimension $3,$ our basis can contain only $1$ vector that lies in $\text{Null}(B-\pi I)^{3}$ but does not lie in $\text{Null}(B-\pi I)^{2}.$

Therefore, there will be 

$$
\text{nullity}(B-\pi I)^{3}-\text{nullity}(B-\pi I)^{2}=3-2=1
$$

["question-ea3ea5b4-3a71-55fd-af96-eb417a578734" :question/problem "Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral 

$$
{∬}_{D}(x-y){e}^{x+y}\,dxdy,
$$

where $D$ is the quadrilateral region with vertices $(0,0),$ $(2,-2),$ $(3,-1),$ and $(1,1).$"] ["question-ea3ea5b4-3a71-55fd-af96-eb417a578734" :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y)=(x-y){e}^{x+y}
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=x-y,\,v=x+y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

The vertices of our domain $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1}(0,0) & =(0-0,0+0) \\  & =(0,0) \\ {T}^{-1}(2,-2) & =(2-(-2),2+(-2)) \\  & =(4,0) \\ {T}^{-1}(3,-1) & =(3-(-1),3+(-1)) \\  & =(4,2) \\ {T}^{-1}(1,1) & =(1-1,1+1) \\  & =(0,2)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 4,\,0\le v\le 2\}
$$

![](images/0b/0b23c6463447aa1fb64bdeeca689a40711f8dad59b348bb7943c2b9d2de7e8fc.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{aligned}| \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2}
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$

"question-ea3ea5b4-3a71-55fd-af96-eb417a578734"] [17592186198596 :question/problem "Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral 

$$
{∬}_{D}(2x-1)(x+y)^{2}\,dxdy,
$$

where $D$ is the quadrilateral region with vertices $(1,0),$ $(2,-1),$ $(2,2),$ and $(1,3).$"] [17592186198596 :question/worked-solution "Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y)=(2x-1)(x+y)^{2}
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=2x-1,\,v=x+y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

The vertices of our domain $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1}(1,0) & =(2(1)-1,1+0) \\  & =(1,1) \\ {T}^{-1}(2,-1) & =(2(2)-1,2+(-1)) \\  & =(3,1) \\ {T}^{-1}(2,2) & =(2(2)-1,2+2) \\  & =(3,4) \\ {T}^{-1}(1,3) & =(2(1)-1,1+3) \\  & =(1,4)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 3,\,1\le v\le 4\}
$$

![](images/1d/1d5943d2cf79e7c77f6db3e939242d7e31068f46506fa618abd24b6ac813d32a.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2}
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2x-1)(x+y)^{2}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}u{v}^{2}\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}u{v}^{2}\,|\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}u{v}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}{v}^{2}\text{d}v{\int }_{1}^{3}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{v}^{3}]}_{1}^{4}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{1}^{3}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 21\cdot 4\,\text{d}v \\  & =42.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186198596 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] [17592186194207 :answer-field/correct 17592186194208] ["activity-5fa958b3-5d69-501f-b05b-9c4db4f578a3" :activity/id #uuid $\text{mm}/\text{s}.$"] ["question-e4e15d3e-925b-56d4-bf57-253dd32acaf7" :question/worked-solution "Let $x,y,z$ be the dimensions of the solid, and let $V$ be its volume. We are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =100\,\text{mm}, \\ y & =60\,\text{mm}, \\ z & =30\,\text{mm}.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-20\,\text{mm}\text{/s}, \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =0\,{\text{mm}}^{3}\text{/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}$ when $x=100\,\text{mm},$ $y=60\,\text{mm}$ and $z=30\,\text{mm}.$

We start with the formula for the volume of the rectangular prism:

$$
V=xyz
$$

Since $y$ is not changing and $y=60,$ we get

$$
V=60xz.
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(60xz) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =60x(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})+60z(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}).\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug in the known values into the above expression. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =60(100)(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})+60(30)(-20) \\ 0 & =6000(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})-36\,000 \\ 36\,000 & =6000(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}) \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t} & =6\,\text{mm}\text{/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the height of the solid is increasing at a rate of $6\,\text{mm}/\text{s}$ at the moment when $x=100\,\text{mm},$ $y=60\,\text{mm}$ and $z=30\,\text{mm}.$"] ["question-e4e15d3e-925b-56d4-bf57-253dd32acaf7" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-b852a09c-ea6b-5010-b9b3-a3b637cbd328" :answer-field/id #uuid "b852a09c-ea6b-5010-b9b3-a3b637cbd328"] ["answer-f9e53027-3a83-5961-948b-e0b5df7093f8" :answer/id #uuid "f9e53027-3a83-5961-948b-e0b5df7093f8"] ["answer-f9e53027-3a83-5961-948b-e0b5df7093f8" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-f9e53027-3a83-5961-948b-e0b5df7093f8" :answer/value "6"] ["answer-field-b852a09c-ea6b-5010-b9b3-a3b637cbd328" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-b852a09c-ea6b-5010-b9b3-a3b637cbd328" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-b852a09c-ea6b-5010-b9b3-a3b637cbd328" :answer-field/correct "answer-f9e53027-3a83-5961-948b-e0b5df7093f8"] ["answer-field-b852a09c-ea6b-5010-b9b3-a3b637cbd328" :answer-field/choices "answer-f9e53027-3a83-5961-948b-e0b5df7093f8"] ["question-e4e15d3e-925b-56d4-bf57-253dd32acaf7" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-b852a09c-ea6b-5010-b9b3-a3b637cbd328"] [17592186064376 :knowledge-point/questions "question-e4e15d3e-925b-56d4-bf57-253dd32acaf7"] ["question-a02e865a-6a6d-5b10-8171-4b544dbd46b3" :question/id #uuid "a02e865a-6a6d-5b10-8171-4b544dbd46b3"] ["question-a02e865a-6a6d-5b10-8171-4b544dbd46b3" :question/math-academy-id "q-2795"] ["question-a02e865a-6a6d-5b10-8171-4b544dbd46b3" :question/problem "![](images/52/52448daf1f9aea06b4ab4713756080ddb3ab465b4fae8f92b65a54c251a81d5e.png)

$$

$$

Also, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-1.5\,\text{feet}\text{/min}, \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t} & =1\,\text{feet}\text{/min}, \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =-9\,{\text{feet}}^{3}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}$ when $x=5\,\text{feet},$ $y=3\,\text{feet},$ and $z=2\,\text{feet}.$

We start with the formula for the volume of the rectangular prism:

$$
V=xyz
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x\cdot y\cdot z) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =xy(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})+xz(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})+yz(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2\,\text{cm}, \\ y & =4\,\text{cm}, \\ z & =7\,\text{cm}, \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-5\,\text{cm}\text{/min}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =11\,\text{cm}\text{/min}, \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t} & =-5\,\text{cm}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
S=2xz+2xy+2yz
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2xz+2xy+2yz) \\ \frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =(2x+2y)(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})+(2x+2z)(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})+(2z+2y)(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}).\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug in the known values into the above expression. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =(2\cdot 2+2\cdot 4)(-5)+(2\cdot 2+2\cdot 7)(11)+(2\cdot 7+2\cdot 4)(-5) \\  & =-60+198-110 \\  & =28\,{\text{cm}}^{2}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}

All of the variables change with time. In particular, we are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t}=48\,{\text{cm}}^{2}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}$ when $x=2\,\text{cm}.$

We want to find the rate of change of $x$ knowing the rate of change of $S.$ So, we start with the formula for the surface area of the cube:

$$
S=6{x}^{2}
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(S) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6{x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =12x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug in the known values into the above expression. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =12x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ 48 & =12(2)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the edges are changing at a rate of $2\,\text{cm}/\text{s}.$"] ["question-4e4521f6-9e6d-5c0e-807a-ed8494a208e7" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] $$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-9\text{ cm/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}$ when $x=40\text{ cm}.$

We start with the formula for the volume of the cube:

$$
V={x}^{3}
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug $x=40$ and $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-9\text{ cm/s}$ into the expression for $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3(40)^{2}\cdot (-9)\, \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =-43\,200.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of the cube is decreasing at a rate of $43\,200{\text{ cm}}^{3}\text{/s}$ at the moment when $x=40\,\text{cm}.$"] ["question-2d8efcf9-a827-5e33-8982-8c950b1390fe" ${\text{m}}^{3}\text{/min}.$"] ["question-94a70c07-52ed-54e0-b434-f6f0663ba853" :question/worked-solution "We define the following variables:

- let $L$ and $W$ be the length and width of the swimming pool, respectively, and

- let $h$ and $V$ be the height and volume of the water, respectively.

Note that $h$ and $V$ change with time, while $L$ and $W$ are constants. 

We are given that

$$
L=32\,\text{m},\,W=12\,\text{m},\,\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}=-0.4\,\text{m}/\text{min}.
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.$

The relation between the two time-dependent variables, $V$ and $h,$ is given by the formula for the volume of water:

$$
V=LWh
$$

We differentiate both sides of $V=LWh$ with respect to $t,$ treating both $L$ and $W$ as constants, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}V & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(LWh) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =LW\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can plug in the known values and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =(32)(12)\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =384\cdot (-0.4) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =-153.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the water is draining out at a rate of $153.6\,{\text{m}}^{3}\text{/min}.$"] ["question-94a70c07-52ed-54e0-b434-f6f0663ba853" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-9eb3869d-baa4-5c43-ac49-35af5641a53b" :answer-field/id #uuid "9eb3869d-baa4-5c43-ac49-35af5641a53b"] ["answer-cfb0f980-6010-5ae0-ac8a-7691fa64a449" :answer/id #uuid "cfb0f980-6010-5ae0-ac8a-7691fa64a449"] ["answer-cfb0f980-6010-5ae0-ac8a-7691fa64a449" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-cfb0f980-6010-5ae0-ac8a-7691fa64a449" :answer/value "153.6"] ["answer-field-9eb3869d-baa4-5c43-ac49-35af5641a53b" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-9eb3869d-baa4-5c43-ac49-35af5641a53b" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-9eb3869d-baa4-5c43-ac49-35af5641a53b" :answer-field/correct "answer-cfb0f980-6010-5ae0-ac8a-7691fa64a449"] ["answer-field-9eb3869d-baa4-5c43-ac49-35af5641a53b" :answer-field/choices "answer-cfb0f980-6010-5ae0-ac8a-7691fa64a449"] ["question-94a70c07-52ed-54e0-b434-f6f0663ba853" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-9eb3869d-baa4-5c43-ac49-35af5641a53b"] [17592186064378 :knowledge-point/questions "question-94a70c07-52ed-54e0-b434-f6f0663ba853"] [17592186064724 :question/problem "![](images/f5/f504ea91bae5d27b3e7b31d697ed06c9e34d838724e8dafac46e69d84de9c3cf.png)

$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.$

The relation between the four variables is given by the formula for the volume of a rectangular prism:

$$
V=LWH
$$

We differentiate both sides of $V=LWH$ with respect to $t,$ using the product rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}V & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(LWH) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =W\cdot H(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}t})+L\cdot H(\frac{\text{d}W}{\text{d}t})+L\cdot W(\frac{\text{d}H}{\text{d}t}).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can plug in the known values and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =(10)(15)(-1)+(15)(15)(-2)+(15)(10)(-4) \\  & =-1\,200{\text{ cm}}^{3}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Jennie fills an aquarium, in the shape of a rectangular prism that is $50\,\text{cm}$ long and $25\,\text{cm}$ wide, with water from a tap. How fast is the volume of water in the aquarium changing if the water level is rising at a rate of $0.2\,\text{cm}/\text{h}?$

- let $L$ and $W$ be the length and width of the aquarium, respectively, and

- let $h$ and $V$ be the height and volume of the water, respectively.

Note that $h$ and $V$ change with time, while $L$ and $W$ are constants. 

We are given that

$$
L=50\,\text{m},\,W=25\,\text{m},\,\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}=0.2\,\text{m}/\text{min}.
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.$

The relation between the two time-dependent variables, $V$ and $h,$ is given by the formula for the volume of water:

$$
V=LWh
$$

We differentiate both sides of $V=LWh$ with respect to $t,$ treating both $L$ and $W$ as constants, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}V & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(LWh) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =LW\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can plug in the known values and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =(50)(25)\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =1250\cdot 0.2 \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =250.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of water in the aquarium is increasing at a rate of $250\,{\text{cm}}^{3}\text{/h}.$"] ["question-68f6bf29-8273-5b7e-a834-752eee067f78" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-abea57b7-3c7f-5d2e-8706-848858e9de5a" :answer-field/id #uuid "abea57b7-3c7f-5d2e-8706-848858e9de5a"] ["answer-d5e820f6-11e5-54c5-8711-692747bbbe70" :answer/id #uuid "d5e820f6-11e5-54c5-8711-692747bbbe70"] ["answer-d5e820f6-11e5-54c5-8711-692747bbbe70" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-d5e820f6-11e5-54c5-8711-692747bbbe70" :answer/value "250"] ["answer-field-abea57b7-3c7f-5d2e-8706-848858e9de5a" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-abea57b7-3c7f-5d2e-8706-848858e9de5a" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-abea57b7-3c7f-5d2e-8706-848858e9de5a" :answer-field/correct "answer-d5e820f6-11e5-54c5-8711-692747bbbe70"] ["answer-field-abea57b7-3c7f-5d2e-8706-848858e9de5a" :answer-field/choices "answer-d5e820f6-11e5-54c5-8711-692747bbbe70"] ["question-68f6bf29-8273-5b7e-a834-752eee067f78" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-abea57b7-3c7f-5d2e-8706-848858e9de5a"] [17592186064378 :knowledge-point/questions "question-68f6bf29-8273-5b7e-a834-752eee067f78"] [17592186064452 :activity/expected-seconds 1080.0] [17592186179474 :question/problem "What is the slope of the line $4x-2y=1?$"] [17592186179474 :question/worked-solution "We can find the slope of the line if we can express its equation in slope-intercept form. $$
\begin{aligned}8x+2y & =-7 \\ 2y & =-8x-7 \\ \frac{2y}{2} & =\frac{-8x-7}{2} \\ y & =\frac{-8x}{2}-\frac{7}{2} \\ y & =-4x-\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

From the slope-intercept equation, we can tell that the slope of the line is $m=-4.$"] ["question-1bd18cb1-6693-5a86-9b4f-9983e714337e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] "question-eaf53385-8d80-57b1-9850-e91d1aa3e647"] [17592186180783 :tutorial/content "To determine the slope of a line that is given in standard form, we need to convert the equation to slope-intercept form.

To demonstrate, let's calculate the slope of the following line:

$$
2x + y = 8
$$

To write this equation in slope-intercept form, we solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+y & =8 \\ 2x+y-2x & =8-2x \\ y & =8-2x \\ y & =-2x+8\end{aligned}
$$

From the slope-intercept equation, we can tell that the slope of the line is $m=-2.$"] [17592186180784 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find the $x$- and $y$-intercepts of the following line:

$$
2x + y = 8
$$

Let's find each of them in turn.

- To find the $x$-intercept, we substitute $y=0$ into the equation and solve for $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+(0) & =8 \\ 2x & =8 \\ \frac{2x}{2} & =\frac{8}{2} \\ x & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the line intersects the $x$-axis at the point $(4,0).$

- To find the $y$-intercept, we substitute $x=0$ into the equation and solve for $y{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(0)+y & =8 \\ y & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the line intersects the $y$-axis at the point $(0,8).$"] [17592186179876 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] ["question-d2926681-2f02-501e-9c4c-db877ffeff07" :question/id #uuid "d2926681-2f02-501e-9c4c-db877ffeff07"] ["question-d2926681-2f02-501e-9c4c-db877ffeff07" :question/math-academy-id "q-83562"] ["question-d2926681-2f02-501e-9c4c-db877ffeff07" :question/problem "In what direction does the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+{x}^{2}y$ decrease most rapidly at the point $(\pi ,0)?$"] ["question-d2926681-2f02-501e-9c4c-db877ffeff07" :question/worked-solution "At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ decreases most rapidly in the direction opposite to that of its gradient.

So, we compute $-∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(\pi ,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}-∇f(x,y) & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+{x}^{2}y)\text{ }i-\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+{x}^{2}y)\text{ }j \\  & =-(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+2xy)\text{ }i-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+{x}^{2})\text{ }j \\ -∇f(\pi ,0) & =-(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡0+2\cdot \pi \cdot 0)\text{ }i+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡0+{\pi }^{2})\text{ }j \\  & =i-{\pi }^{2}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function decreases most rapidly in the direction of $i-{\pi }^{2}\,j.$"] ["question-d2926681-2f02-501e-9c4c-db877ffeff07" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] $g(x,y)=\frac{{e}^{y}}{yx}.$ What is the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(1,1)$ in the direction of the vector $v=⟨2,4⟩?$"] ["question-a3fef551-e9bd-56f6-a5fb-6131de39b9cb" :question/worked-solution "The rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(1,1)$ in the direction of $v$ is equal to the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(1,1).$ 

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{4}^{2}}=\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt{5} \\ u & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}⟨2,4⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the gradient $∇g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{e}^{y}}{yx}),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{e}^{y}}{yx})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{{e}^{y}}{{x}^{2}y},\,\frac{{e}^{y}(y-1)}{x{y}^{2}}⟩ \\ ∇g(1,1) & =⟨-\frac{{e}^{1}}{{1}^{2}\cdot 1},\,\frac{{e}^{1}\cdot (1-1)}{1\cdot {1}^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨-e,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(1,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{u}^{′}(1,1) & =∇g(1,1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨-e,0⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨1,2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(-e\cdot 1+0\cdot 2) \\  & =-\frac{e}{\sqrt{5}} \\  & =-\frac{e\sqrt{5}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-a3fef551-e9bd-56f6-a5fb-6131de39b9cb" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-fcae1503-ee5b-5bcc-859b-64edce5a1f65" :answer-field/id #uuid $$"] [17592186342239 :question/worked-solution "We know that $b\in \text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ if there exist ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2} & =b \\ {x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -3 \\ k\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}5{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-3 \\ {x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=-3 \\ 2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=k\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}5 & 1 & -3 \\ 1 & -1 & -3 \\ 2 & -1 & k\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -3 \\ 5 & 1 & -3 \\ 2 & -1 & k\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-5{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -3 \\ 0 & 6 & 12 \\ 2 & -1 & k\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -3 \\ 0 & 6 & 12 \\ 0 & 1 & k+6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{6}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & k+6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & k+4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The third row of the augmented matrix now corresponds to the equation $0{x}_{1}+0{x}_{2}=k+4.$ Therefore, the system has a solution only if

$$

You may assume that flaws appear independently and at a constant average rate."] ["question-7f6be4fe-78ba-5d67-91ec-fd3e20928e4b" :question/worked-solution "A Poisson random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda $ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{\lambda }^{x}{e}^{-\lambda }}{x!}
$$

Let $X$ be the number of flaws in a meter length of the material. Since the average rate is $1.7$ flaws per meter, and events occur independently and at a constant average rate, the number of flaws can be modeled as a Poisson random variable with rate $\lambda =1.7,$ and we can write $X∼\text{Po}(1.7).$

So, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{1.7}^{x}{e}^{-1.7}}{x!}
$$

Therefore, the probability of finding fewer than $4$  flaws in the next meter length of the material is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<4) & =P(X\in \{0,1,2,3\}) \\  & =f(0)+f(1)+f(2)+f(3) \\  & =\frac{{1.7}^{0}{e}^{-1.7}}{0!}+\frac{{1.7}^{1}{e}^{-1.7}}{1!}+\frac{{1.7}^{2}{e}^{-1.7}}{2!}+\frac{{1.7}^{3}{e}^{-1.7}}{3!} \\  & ≈0.907\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places."] ["question-7f6be4fe-78ba-5d67-91ec-fd3e20928e4b" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-7c8ed450-14d6-56b8-9f85-42f0c5090225" :answer-field/id However, if the domain of the variable is restricted, some expressions might allow further simplification. 

For example, suppose we know that $a>0.$ Let's use this information to fully simplify $\sqrt{36a^2}.$

We can start by simplifying the expression as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{36{a}^{2}} & = \\ \sqrt{(6a)^{2}} & = \\ |6a| & = \\ |6|\cdot |a| \\ 6|a| & \end{aligned}
$$

We are told that $a>0,$ and we know that the absolute value of any positive number is just itself, so we have $|a|=a.$ Therefore, our final answer is

$$
6|a| = 6a .
$$"] [17592186180736 :tutorial/content "Let's see what changes if we consider square roots of perfect squares when some variables are negative.

For example, suppose that $t \lt 0.$ Let's use this to simplify the expression $\sqrt{t^2}.$

Simplifying this expression in the usual way, we obtain

$$
\eqalign{
	\sqrt{t^2}&=\[5pt]
	\sqrt{(t)^2}&=\[5pt]
	|t|.&
	}
$$

We're given that $t \lt 0.$ To take the absolute value of a negative number, we need to flip the sign. This gives $|t| = -t.$ Therefore, our final answer is

$$
{\color{blue}\sqrt{t^2}} = {\color{red}-t}.
$$

You can convince yourself that this is correct by plugging a few values of $t$ into the above equation. Provided that $t$ is negative, this expression will always give a true statement.

For example, suppose that $t = -2.$ Substituting into the left-hand side of the equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{t}^{2}} & = \\ \sqrt{(-2)^{2}} & = \\ \sqrt{4} & = \\ 2 & .\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $t=-2$ into the right-hand side of the equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-t & = \\ -(-2) & = \\ 2 & .\end{aligned}
$$

Since both sides give the same result, the statement is true."] [17592186179879 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] ["question-3a497a8c-181f-5ddb-8e0c-d7f0dcc66829" :question/id #uuid "3a497a8c-181f-5ddb-8e0c-d7f0dcc66829"] ["question-3a497a8c-181f-5ddb-8e0c-d7f0dcc66829" :question/math-academy-id "q-38861"] ["question-3a497a8c-181f-5ddb-8e0c-d7f0dcc66829" :question/problem "Suppose $T:V\to W$ is a linear map and $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ and $C=\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$ are the bases of the vector spaces $V$ and $W$, respectively. :question/problem "Consider the basis $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ of the vector space $V$ and the basis $C$ of ${R}^{2}$ given by

$$
C=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -4\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Find the matrix $[T]_{B|C}$ of the map $T:V\to {R}^{2}$ relative to these bases if 

$$
T({b}_{1})=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,T({b}_{2})=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$"] ["question-00e54e6a-cd0f-51b4-97b3-2489c07dd2c2" :question/worked-solution "Recall that $[T]_{B|C}$ is the matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors $T({b}_{1})$ and $T({b}_{2})$ relative to the basis $C.$

First, we need to find the coordinates of $T({b}_{i})$ relative to the basis $C$ for each $i=1,2.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the following matrix:

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & T({b}_{1}) & T({b}_{2}) \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

We reduce the left-hand side to reduced row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & -1 \\ -4 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -3 & 9 & -3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=(-\frac{1}{3}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the right-hand side gives the matrix of the linear transformation relative to the bases $B$ and $C:$

$$
[T]_{B|C}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$"] ["question-00e54e6a-cd0f-51b4-97b3-2489c07dd2c2" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-f4374709-dd94-564d-a093-c34e0f6d470b" :answer-field/id #uuid \{\begin{aligned}s-8t=6 \\ 7s+10t=9 \\ -3s-4t=-4\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$

$$
u=2b-\frac{1}{2}c.

["question-3bf6c999-4f9a-599b-886e-437d5517ddbb" :question/worked-solution "We need to find a matrix $E$ such that $EA$ is equivalent to applying the elementary row operation ${R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}$ to $$
\begin{aligned}I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =E\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equivalent notation in terms of matrix multiplication is $EA:$

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot A
$$"] ["question-3bf6c999-4f9a-599b-886e-437d5517ddbb" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-07dcfd9e-686a-5980-8030-4e14ec2230eb" :answer-field/id #uuid "step-6480aa5b-ee2d-59de-9bc0-5718af92cb12"] [17592186068432 :question/problem "Simplify $\sqrt{8z^3}.$"] [17592186068432 :question/worked-solution "We first write $8z^3$ as the product $4z^2 \cdot 2z$ which contains a perfect square $(4z^2){:}$ 

$$
\eqalign{
	\sqrt{8z^3}&=\[3pt]
	\sqrt{4z^2 \cdot 2z}&
	}
$$

Then, we can separate the product into two separate radicals:

$$
\eqalign{
	\sqrt{4z^2 \cdot 2z}&=\[3pt]
        \sqrt{(2z)^2\cdot 2z}&=\[3pt]
        \sqrt{(2z)^2}\cdot \sqrt{2z}&
	}
$$

Finally, we simplify the radical containing the perfect square:

$$
\eqalign{
        \sqrt{(2z)^2}\cdot \sqrt{2z}&=\[3pt]
        |2z|\cdot \sqrt{2z}&=\[3pt]
        |2|\cdot|z|\cdot \sqrt{2z}&=\[3pt]
	2|z|\sqrt{2z}&
	}
$$"] [17592186068676 :question/problem "Simplify $\sqrt{50u^7}.$"] [17592186068676 :question/worked-solution "We first write $50u^7$ as the product $25u^6\cdot 2u$ which contains a perfect square $(25u^6){:}$ 

$$
\eqalign{
	\sqrt{50u^7}&=\[3pt]
	\sqrt{25u^6\cdot 2u}&
	}
$$

Then, we separate the product into two separate radicals:

$$
\eqalign{
	\sqrt{25u^6\cdot 2u}&=\[3pt]
	\sqrt{\left(5u^3\right)^2\cdot 2u}&=\[3pt]
	\sqrt{\left(5u^3\right)^2}\cdot\sqrt{2u}&
	}
$$

Finally, we simplify the radical containing the perfect square:

$$
\eqalign{
	\sqrt{\left(5u^3\right)^2}\cdot\sqrt{2u}&=\[3pt]
	|5u^3|\cdot\sqrt{2u}&=\[3pt]
	|5|\cdot |u^3|\cdot\sqrt{2u}&=\[3pt]
	5|u|^3 \sqrt{2u}
	}
$$"] [17592186068469 :question/problem "Simplify $\sqrt{18y^3}$ given that $y \geq 0.$"] [17592186068469 :question/worked-solution "We first write $18y^3$ as the product $9y^2\cdot 2y$ which contains a perfect square $(9y^2).$ Then, we separate the product into two separate radicals, one of which can be simplified:

$$
\eqalign{
		\sqrt{18y^3} &= \
		\sqrt{9y^2 \cdot 2y} &= \				
		\sqrt{9y^2} \cdot \sqrt{2y} &= \		
		\sqrt{(3y)^2} \cdot \sqrt{2y} &= \		
		|3y| \cdot \sqrt{2y} &= \		
		|3| \cdot |y| \cdot \sqrt{2y} &= \
		3 \cdot |y| \cdot \sqrt{2y}
	}
$$

Since $y \geq 0,$ we have $|y|=y,$ and we can simplify further. Therefore, our final answer is

$$
\eqalign{
		3 \cdot |y| \cdot \sqrt{2y} &= \
		3 \cdot y \cdot \sqrt{2y} &= \
		3y\sqrt{2y}. &
	}
$$"] ["question-0902afad-f2ba-5dbf-8fa2-d595df73885c" :question/id #uuid "0902afad-f2ba-5dbf-8fa2-d595df73885c"] ["question-0902afad-f2ba-5dbf-8fa2-d595df73885c" :question/math-academy-id "q-141778"] ["question-0902afad-f2ba-5dbf-8fa2-d595df73885c" :question/problem "Simplify $\sqrt{25{r}^{3}}.$"] ["question-0902afad-f2ba-5dbf-8fa2-d595df73885c" :question/worked-solution "We first write $25{r}^{3}$ as the product $25{r}^{2}\cdot r$ which contains a perfect square $(25{r}^{2}):$

Then, we can separate the product into two separate radicals:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{25{r}^{2}\cdot r} & = \\ \sqrt{(5r)^{2}\cdot r} & = \\ \sqrt{(5r)^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{r} & \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify the radical containing the perfect square:

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{144{b}^{7}} & = \\ \sqrt{144{b}^{6}\cdot b} & \end{aligned}
$$

Then, we separate the product into two separate radicals:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{144{b}^{6}\cdot b} & = \\ \sqrt{{(12{b}^{3})}^{2}\cdot b} & = \\ \sqrt{{(12{b}^{3})}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{b} & \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify the radical containing the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{(12{b}^{3})}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{b} & = \\ |12{b}^{3}|\cdot \sqrt{b} & = \\ |12|\cdot |{b}^{3}|\cdot \sqrt{b} & = \\ 12|b{|}^{3}\sqrt{b}\end{aligned}

:question/problem "Simplify $\sqrt{8{a}^{2}}$ given that $a\ge 0.$"] ["question-1704928a-5b6a-5e32-992c-5da9fe38c678" :question/worked-solution "We first write $8{a}^{2}$ as the product $4{a}^{2}\cdot 2$ which contains a perfect square $(4{a}^{2}).$ Then, we can separate the product into two separate radicals, one of which can be simplified:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{8{a}^{2}} & = \\ \sqrt{4{a}^{2}\cdot 2} & = \\ \sqrt{(2a)^{2}\cdot 2} & = \\ \sqrt{(2a)^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{2} & = \\ |2a|\sqrt{2} & = \\ |2|\cdot |a|\cdot \sqrt{2} & = \\ 2\cdot |a|\cdot \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $a\ge 0,$ we have $|a|=a,$ and we can simplify further. Therefore, our final answer is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\cdot |a|\cdot \sqrt{2} & = \\ 2\cdot a\cdot \sqrt{2} & = \\ 2a\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-1704928a-5b6a-5e32-992c-5da9fe38c678" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-2d6498f4-a70b-50c1-9ce5-2cc3f0cc3064" :answer-field/id #uuid "question-1704928a-5b6a-5e32-992c-5da9fe38c678"] [17592186069224 :question/problem "Simplify $\sqrt{32{y}^{3}}$ given that $y\ge 0.$"] [17592186069224 :question/worked-solution "We first write $32{y}^{3}$ as the product $16{y}^{2}\cdot 2y$ which contains a perfect square $(16{y}^{2}).$ Then, we separate the product into two separate radicals, one of which can be simplified:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{32{y}^{3}} & = \\ \sqrt{16{y}^{2}\cdot 2y} & = \\ \sqrt{(4y)^{2}\cdot 2y} & = \\ \sqrt{(4y)^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{2y} & = \\ |4y|\cdot \sqrt{2y} & = \\ |4|\cdot |y|\cdot \sqrt{2y} & = \\ 4\cdot |y|\cdot \sqrt{2y}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $y\ge 0,$ we have $|y|=y,$ and we can simplify further. Therefore, our final answer is

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot |y|\cdot \sqrt{2y} & = \\ 4\cdot y\cdot \sqrt{2y} & = \\ 4y\sqrt{2y}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186069224 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-effe64da-d5ba-51cb-959c-be6a879f598d" :answer/id #uuid "effe64da-d5ba-51cb-959c-be6a879f598d"] ["answer-effe64da-d5ba-51cb-959c-be6a879f598d" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-effe64da-d5ba-51cb-959c-be6a879f598d" :answer/value "2{y}^{2}\sqrt{8y}"] [17592186066522 :answer-field/correct 17592186066526] [17592186066522 :answer-field/choices "answer-effe64da-d5ba-51cb-959c-be6a879f598d"] [17592186069943 :tutorial/content "The **product rule for radicals** states that the square root of a product equals the product of the square roots:

$$
\eqalign{
		\sqrt{ab} &=\sqrt{a} \cdot \sqrt{b}
	}
$$

We can use the product rule to rewrite the square roots of algebraic expressions.

As an example, let's suppose we want to simplify the following expression:

$$
\sqrt{32y}
$$

First, we rewrite $32y$ as the product $16 \cdot 2y,$ which contains a perfect square $(16){:}$ 

$$
\eqalign{
	\sqrt{32y}&=\[5pt]
	\sqrt{16 \cdot 2y}&=\[5pt]
	\sqrt{4^2 \cdot 2y}&

	}
$$

Then, we separate the product into two separate radicals using the product rule:

$$
\eqalign{
        \sqrt{4^2\cdot 2y}&=\[3pt]
        \sqrt{4^2}\cdot \sqrt{2y}&
	}
$$

Finally, we simplify the radical containing the perfect square:

$$
\eqalign{
        \sqrt{4^2}\cdot \sqrt{2y}&=\[3pt]
        |4|\cdot \sqrt{2y}&=\[3pt]

	4\sqrt{2y}&
	}
$$"] [17592186068936 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0] ["question-770dc96c-77d3-556b-b303-18d387043365" :question/id #uuid "770dc96c-77d3-556b-b303-18d387043365"] ["question-770dc96c-77d3-556b-b303-18d387043365" :question/math-academy-id "q-89606"] ["question-770dc96c-77d3-556b-b303-18d387043365" :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{75}x,\, & 5\le x\le 10 \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

its cumulative distribution function is 

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0,\, & x<5 \\ h(x),\, & 5\le x\le 10 \\ 1,\, & x>10.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the function $h(x).$"] ["question-770dc96c-77d3-556b-b303-18d387043365" :question/worked-solution "Since our random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that is strictly positive only for $5\le x\le 10,$ the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<5 \\ {\int }_{5}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t, & 5\le x\le 10 \\ 1, & x>10\end{aligned}
$$

For the given probability density function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{5}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{5}^{x}\frac{2}{75}t\,\text{d}t \\ \text{ } & ={\frac{1}{75}{t}^{2}|}_{5}^{x} \\  & =\frac{1}{75}{x}^{2}-\frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}-25}{75}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0,\, & x<5, \\ \frac{{x}^{2}-25}{75},\, & 5\le x\le 10, \\ 1,\, & x>10.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-770dc96c-77d3-556b-b303-18d387043365" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-94adf626-a400-5181-b287-7ccffcedb8aa" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

$$
f(x)=\frac{3{x}^{2}}{\pi (1+{x}^{6})},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

find the cumulative distribution function $F(x).$"] ["question-b31007d2-c9e1-51d3-8e66-44402735c224" :question/worked-solution "The cumulative distribution function of a continuous random variable $X$ is the function $F(x)$ defined by

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)={\int }_{-\infty }^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

For the given probability density function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{3{t}^{2}}{\pi (1+{t}^{6})}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\frac{\operatorname{arctan}⁡({t}^{3})}{\pi }|}_{-\infty }^{x} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{arctan}⁡({x}^{3})}{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-b31007d2-c9e1-51d3-8e66-44402735c224" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-b07d72d2-93c7-594a-8963-dcc12be62f0b" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)=\frac{{e}^{-|x|}}{2},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

its cumulative distribution function is

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}^{x}}{2},\, & x\le 0 \\ h(x),\, & x>0\end{aligned}
$$

where $h(x)=${{field-1}}."] ["question-d0e0e171-2942-5666-9f4c-984a9e7d868a" :question/worked-solution "Since our random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that involves an absolute value, the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\{\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{t}}{2}\,\text{d}t, & x<0 \\ {\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t}}{2}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t}}{2}\,\text{d}t, & x\ge 0\end{aligned}
$$

Let's compute the integrals.

- If $x\le 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{t}}{2}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{t}}{2}|}_{-\infty }^{x} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{x}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t}}{2}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{x}}{2}|}_{x=0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t}}{2}\,\text{d}t & =-{\frac{{e}^{-t}}{2}|}_{0}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t}}{2}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t}}{2}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}+(-\frac{{e}^{-x}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =1-\frac{{e}^{-x}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}^{x}}{2},\, & x\le 0 \\ 1-\frac{{e}^{-x}}{2},\, & x>0.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-d0e0e171-2942-5666-9f4c-984a9e7d868a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-bb588555-9fd1-5660-8555-bc1960f97262" :answer-field/id #uuid "![](images/0f/0f178c33254644c5e2e7bf6f3c596df87b1ea2f0b5bfd417c3f279f6c62b1b0d.png)

Consider the circle $S$ and the vector field $F,$ shown above. Let $C$ be any path where $S$ is traversed once in the **clockwise** direction. Which of the following statements are true?

I. ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$

II. ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0$

III. ${∮}_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$"] ["question-5f7aceb3-5a6a-584b-8488-47f8fb82e9a0" :question/worked-solution "The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

We now recall the following:

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is false, while statement II is true. It's clear from the picture below that $F$ works against the motion of the particle as it moves clockwise along $C.$ 

![](images/f8/f87d2e735ad58e0b33a813fb91ab202ac0eeaf90575979ea45f954fb7e1d0493.png)

So, $Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

- Statement III is true. It's clear from the picture below that $F$ assists the motion of the particle as it moves counterclockwise along $C.$

![](images/10/102c11f9002e29a3759679c6ff0bd10188908d33eb9cc94a84d900956adc33a5.png)

So, $Γ={∮}_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only.""] ["question-5f7aceb3-5a6a-584b-8488-47f8fb82e9a0" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate]
