You may assume that typos occur independently and at a constant average rate." :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "A Poisson random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda $ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{\lambda }^{x}{e}^{-\lambda }}{x!}
$$

Let $X$ be the number of typos on a page of the book. Since the average rate is $4$ typos per page, and events occur independently and at a constant average rate, the number of typos can be modeled as a Poisson random variable with rate $\lambda =4,$ and we can write $X∼\text{Po}(4).$

So, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{4}^{x}{e}^{-4}}{x!}
$$

Therefore, the probability of finding $2$ typos on the next page is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=2) & =f(2) \\  & =\frac{{4}^{2}{e}^{-4}}{2!} \\  & ≈0.147\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186157855 :question/id #uuid "f2f829d4-b2e4-56da-a356-3f1328031b01" :question/math-academy-id "q-85151"} {:db/id 17592186419532 :question/id #uuid "15726506-9b26-5fcb-965d-d1bfeaeef6e9" :question/math-academy-id "q-131266"} {:db/id 17592186419536 :question/id #uuid "5019f447-273c-518d-a2e4-ccc53ac4a221" :question/math-academy-id "q-85325"} {:db/id 17592186419539 :question/id #uuid "7876349f-b735-5751-9a1b-0e3749e49e68" :question/math-academy-id "q-85324"} {:db/id 17592186419540 :question/id #uuid "840811f2-e29f-518b-8c90-d58cbee9a3ee" :question/math-academy-id "q-85329"} {:db/id 17592186419544 :question/id #uuid "dddb9707-e886-593b-b435-6f7cb6f00a64" :question/math-academy-id "q-131269"} {:db/id 17592186437136 :question/id #uuid "033d05af-1912-5a6e-86f3-f9dda400af0a" :question/math-academy-id "q-131102" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "103af267-4448-5f1d-b2c7-5d3a6eb5caa1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.132" :db/id 17592186437113} {:answer/id #uuid "5546866d-cf0c-5f34-a20b-0d37698b92d2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.050" :db/id 17592186437119} {:answer/id #uuid "7a864749-ecf3-5067-80f4-653b14e5fe85" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.018" :db/id 17592186437121} {:answer/id #uuid "9cc7c554-abbe-5a01-96eb-fd4a8610edf5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.122" :db/id 17592186437125} {:answer/id #uuid "d4920049-b97d-5e34-bd87-a602c7c19c73" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.034" :db/id 17592186437128}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186437119} :answer-field/id #uuid "c35bc065-fcec-52cb-96c4-b81be5324354" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186437135}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "A company rents cars to tourists. You may assume that bacteria appear independently and at a constant average rate." :question/worked-solution "A Poisson random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda $ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{\lambda }^{x}{e}^{-\lambda }}{x!}
$$

Let $X$ be the number of bacteria in one milliliter of the liquid. Since the average rate is $6$ bacteria per milliliter, and events occur independently and at a constant average rate, the number of bacteria can be modeled as a Poisson random variable with rate $\lambda =6,$ and we can write $X∼\text{Po}(6).$

So, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{6}^{x}{e}^{-6}}{x!}
$$

Therefore, the probability that at most $3$ bacteria will be found in one milliliter of the liquid is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 3) & =P(X\in \{0,1,2,3\}) \\  & =f(0)+f(1)+f(2)+f(3) \\  & =\frac{{6}^{0}{e}^{-6}}{0!}+\frac{{6}^{1}{e}^{-6}}{1!}+\frac{{6}^{2}{e}^{-6}}{2!}+\frac{{6}^{3}{e}^{-6}}{3!} \\  & ≈0.151\end{aligned}
$$

You may assume that calls occur independently and at a constant average rate." :question/worked-solution "A Poisson random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda $ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{\lambda }^{x}{e}^{-\lambda }}{x!}
$$

Let $X$ be the number of calls received in the telephone exchange. Since the average rate is $7$ calls every $5$ minutes, and events occur independently and at a constant average rate, the number of calls can be modeled as a Poisson random variable with rate $\lambda =7,$ and we can write $X∼\text{Po}(7).$ 

So, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{7}^{x}{e}^{-7}}{x!}
$$

To compute $P(X\ge 5),$ we will use the complement:

$$
P(X\ge 5)=1-P(X<5)
$$

Computing the probability of the complement, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<5) & =P(X\in \{0,1,2,3,4\}) \\  & =f(0)+f(1)+f(2)+f(3)+f(4) \\  & =\frac{{7}^{0}{e}^{-7}}{0!}+\frac{{7}^{1}{e}^{-7}}{1!}+\frac{{7}^{2}{e}^{-7}}{2!}+\frac{{7}^{3}{e}^{-7}}{3!}+\frac{{7}^{4}{e}^{-7}}{4!} \\  & ≈0.173\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

Therefore, the probability of receiving at least $5$ calls in the next $5$ minutes is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 5) & =1-P(X<5) \\  & ≈1-0.173 \\  & =0.827\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186048674} {:db/id 17592186049302} {:db/id 17592186049414} {:db/id 17592186048731 :topic/difficulty 0.5530390729701514 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186428829 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. We can compute the variance of $X$ using the following formula:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}

We start by computing $\text{E}[{X}^{2}].$ Summing up the products of each value of ${X}^{2}$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={0}^{2}\cdot f(0)+{2}^{2}\cdot f(2)+{4}^{2}\cdot f(4) \\  & =4\cdot \frac{1}{3}+16\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{20}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{20}{3}-{2}^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\sqrt{3}X] & =3\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =3\cdot \frac{8}{3} \\  & =8.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

| $f(x)$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{5}{8}$ |" :question/worked-solution "Recall that for any random variable $X$ and constant $a,$ we have

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\frac{1}{2}X] & ={(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \text{Var}[X].\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the variance of $X$ using the following formula:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}
$$

Additionally, we're given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{9}{2}.$ 

We start by computing $\text{E}[{X}^{2}].$ Summing up the products of each value of ${X}^{2}$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={0}^{2}\cdot f(0)+{3}^{2}\cdot f(3)+{6}^{2}\cdot f(6) \\  & =9\cdot \frac{1}{4}+36\cdot \frac{5}{8} \\  & =\frac{99}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{99}{4}-{(\frac{9}{2})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[2-5X] & =(-5)^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =25\cdot \text{Var}[X].\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={5}^{2}\cdot f(5)+{6}^{2}\cdot f(6)+{9}^{2}\cdot f(9) \\  & =25(\frac{1}{5})+36(\frac{2}{5})+81(\frac{2}{5}) \\  & =\frac{259}{5}.\end{aligned}

of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ is

$$
U = \left\{ x_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + x_2 \mathbf{a}_2 \: : \: x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R} \right\}.
$$

The set $U$ is also called the **linear span** of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2,$ and is denoted by $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}.$ We say that $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ are the **generators** of $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}.$

For example, let's find the linear span generated by the following vectors:
![](images/55/55c749dccc54c252b9120f148e383f395c09fb4cd4bec0e1cce8ed441ecb6199.svg)

From the definition of linear span, we know that if $\mathbf{b} \in \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \},$ then $\mathbf{b}$ must take the form

$$
\mathbf{b} = x_1\mathbf{a_1} + x_2\mathbf{a_2}
$$

 for some $x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R}.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}b & ={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the linear span of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ is
![](images/21/2181b471f34906eeaea7889abbba37c797a2f9624cee455b43b00fc048247cd1.svg)

Geometrically, $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}$ can be viewed as the plane $\Pi$ that passes through the origin and is parallel to the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2,$ as shown below.

- The span of a single nonzero vector is a *line* through the origin. More precisely, if $\mathbf{a} \neq \mathbf{0},$ then $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a} \}$ determines the *line* with direction vector $\mathbf{a}$ that passes through the origin. For instance, if
![](images/dd/ddef437718d3a11811da02a17e2207d75e2d1852eeada67ab494af45b2a655e2.svg)
then $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a} \}$ represents the line $l$ *spanned* by $\mathbf{a}\mathbin{:}$

![](images/08/080aa6203494e915e28c491a3d86176f7ba634bcbdfe40b094c07d85fb29bb69.png)

- The span of two non-parallel vectors is a *plane* through the origin. More precisely, if $\mathbf{a} \not\parallel \mathbf{b}$ ($\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are not parallel), then $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \}$ determines the *plane* with direction vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ that passes through the origin. For instance, if

then $\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \}$  represents the plane $\Pi$ *spanned* by $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

$$

:question/math-academy-id "q-34636" :question/problem "Find the values of $k$ such that the vector $b$ lies in $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2 \\ 8\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -8 \\ k\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/worked-solution "We know that $b\in \text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ if there exist ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2} & =b \\ {x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2 \\ 8\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -8 \\ k\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=-2 \\ -2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=-8 \\ 8{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=k\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2 & -8 \\ 8 & 2 & k\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -8 \\ 4 & 2 & -2 \\ 8 & 2 & k\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -8 \\ 0 & 6 & -18 \\ 8 & 2 & k\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -8 \\ 0 & 6 & -18 \\ 0 & 10 & k-32\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{6}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -8 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & 10 & k-32\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-10{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & -8 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & k-2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The third row of the augmented matrix now corresponds to the equation $0{x}_{1}+0{x}_{2}=k-2.$ Therefore, the system has a solution only if

$$
0=k-2\,⟹\,k=2.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "19ecde81-ba5d-52b8-b7b7-9282a3f95b93" :step/next {:db/id 17592186436142}} {:db/id 17592186436140 :step/content {:db/id 17592186342237 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00ea0212-0c8f-50de-a9e9-986f267bdb5a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186339138} {:answer/id #uuid "25b09d72-beeb-56f8-b3c5-bd45509568ea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-16" :db/id 17592186339451} {:answer/id #uuid "392acaa5-a047-5743-bd68-0e133d8bead9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186339642} {:answer/id #uuid "c4734975-ddc9-5119-b9e9-59e873e223ff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-18" :db/id 17592186340873} {:answer/id #uuid "d55e6034-4f45-5b74-b206-75e90bc1aef4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186341016}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186339138} :answer-field/id #uuid "690b25a1-892c-577b-b6f7-6ff437d6dcd1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341563}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "e12a2efc-9d88-56c5-96b5-ec530d76269d" :question/math-academy-id "q-74594" :question/problem "Find the values of $k$ such that the vector $b$ lies in $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\},$ where

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$

The third row of the augmented matrix now corresponds to the equation $0{x}_{1}+0{x}_{2}=k-6.$ Therefore, the system has a solution only if

$$
\begin{aligned}sb+tc & =u \\ s[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -5 \\ -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-s+2t=5 \\ 3s-t=-5 \\ 2s-t=-4\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 5 \\ 3 & -1 & -5 \\ 2 & -1 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 5 & 10 \\ 2 & -1 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 5 & 10 \\ 0 & 3 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{5}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-s+2t=5 \\ t=2 \\ 0=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get

$$
t=2.
$$

Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-s+2t & =5 \\ -s+2(2) & =5 \\ -s+4 & =5 \\ s & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we found a solution $s=-1,\,t=2,$ we conclude that $u$ does indeed lie on the plane $Π.$ In fact, we have

$$
u=-b+2c.
$$

Finally, $s\cdot t=(-1)\cdot 2=-2.$"} :step/id #uuid "70ef282b-5ccd-5b1e-a1f8-1bcffa1e4789" :step/next {:db/id 17592186436143}} {:db/id 17592186436142 :step/content {:db/id 17592186342228 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "28049f08-5684-5304-ad3d-9f534b59f279" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186339478} {:answer/id #uuid "67519cd7-cc6e-5952-bf35-4a4a24da747e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "15" :db/id 17592186340043} {:answer/id #uuid "79c14b9a-0376-5405-a220-fdac02f464da" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186340214} {:answer/id #uuid "92c70a7d-6a91-5cb6-8d17-c5ff99a5580f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-6" :db/id 17592186340448} {:answer/id #uuid "b383d39f-e410-5314-b906-611aa1b45702" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186340760}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186340043} :answer-field/id #uuid "b6c41871-59a4-56ef-80fe-7d004904e3a0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341700}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "62066547-f160-5da7-be83-cd71028d6d36" :question/math-academy-id "q-74556" :question/problem "Find the values of $k$ such that the vector $b$ lies in $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\},$ where

\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 5 \\ 3 & -1 & -5 \\ 2 & -1 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 5 & 10 \\ 2 & -1 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 5 & 10 \\ 0 & 3 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{5}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-s+2t=5 \\ t=2 \\ 0=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get

$$
t=2.
$$

Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-s+2t & =5 \\ -s+2(2) & =5 \\ -s+4 & =5 \\ s & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we found a solution $s=-1,\,t=2,$ we conclude that $u$ does indeed lie on the plane $Π.$ In fact, we have

$$
u=-b+2c.
$$

Finally, $s\cdot t=(-1)\cdot 2=-2.$"} :step/id #uuid "70ef282b-5ccd-5b1e-a1f8-1bcffa1e4789" :step/next {:db/id 17592186436143}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid $u=sb+tc.$" :question/worked-solution "By definition, $u\in Π$ if there exist $t$ and $s$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}sb+tc & =u \\ s[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -8 \\ 14\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -10 \\ -14\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-s-3t=5 \\ -s-8t=-10 \\ 4s+14t=-14\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the system above, we set up and row reduce an augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 & 5 \\ -1 & -8 & -10 \\ 4 & 14 & -14\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 & 5 \\ 0 & -5 & -15 \\ 4 & 14 & -14\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 & 5 \\ 0 & -5 & -15 \\ 0 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{5}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-s-3t=5 \\ t=3 \\ 0=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get

$$
t=3.
$$

Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-s-3t & =5 \\ -s-3(3) & =5 \\ -s-9 & =5 \\ s & =-14.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we found a solution $s=-14,\,t=3,$ we conclude that $u$ does indeed lie on the plane $Π.$ In fact, we have

$$
u=-14b+3c.
$$

Finally, $s\cdot t=(-14)\cdot 3=-42.$"} :step/id #uuid "acd92085-628d-5fd7-8ceb-59efc32f4636"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "28049f08-5684-5304-ad3d-9f534b59f279" :answer/type {:db/id :tutorial/content "Remember the following three standard elementary row operations: 

  I. Swapping two rows

  II. Multiplying a row by a non-zero number

  III. Adding a multiple of one row to another row

Of these three elementary row operations, only III (adding a multiple of one row to another row) *preserves* the determinant. The other two operations, switching two rows or multiplying a row by a non-zero number, *change* the determinant.

To demonstrate, let's consider the matrix ![](images/fa/fa51d7c585db408c47e8640ae839c1a3bbf94e2b0097e1ade511e5773461f1e8.svg) Taking the determinant, we have
![](images/bc/bcf5c5dc9f5b7ed3849e719665f802040cf51e3334ae99e25ea7648cbb0f6134.svg)

If we swap the two rows, we get a different determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}| & =3\cdot 2-1\cdot 4 \\  & =2 \\  & \ne -2\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Likewise, if we multiply top row by ${\color{red}2},$ then we get a different determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2\cdot 1 & 2\cdot 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\cdot 4-3\cdot 4 \\  & =-4 \\  & \ne -2\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

However, if we add twice the top row to the bottom row, then we get the same determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3+2\cdot 1 & 4+2\cdot 2\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 5 & 8\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot 8-2\cdot 5 \\  & =-2\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e5ae8e63-4d2c-5491-9908-96fe94243ab9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3004 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "57d74627-70e0-5830-ba95-6cb026f4de4b" :step/math-academy-id "9c7f038a-e114-5e98-bc36-49762d4031f6" :step/math-academy-id 16216 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120742}} {:db/id 17592186120629 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121021 :tutorial/content "Since $\det(A^T)=\det(A),$ the corresponding elementary column operations on determinants have the same properties as the elementary row ones.

- Swapping two columns changes the sign of the determinant.

- Multiplying a column by a number scales the determinant by that number.

- Adding a multiple of one column to another column does not change the determinant." :tutorial/id #uuid "bac0b72b-b76a-5a06-9312-d2b7b8ac4247" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3005 :tutorial/title "Column Operations on Determinants"} :step/id #uuid "d5da1bd5-0cc1-56fe-a8d7-36aa6576326a" :step/math-academy-id 16217} {:db/id 17592186120703 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121044 :tutorial/content "As we saw, swapping two rows does not preserve the determinant. However, the only difference is the sign of the determinant changes. 

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}| & =1\cdot 4-2\cdot 3=-2 \\ |\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}| & =3\cdot 2-1\cdot 4=2\end{aligned}
$$

So, in the above example, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}| & =-|\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In general, swapping any two rows of a matrix changes the sign of the determinant to the opposite one. That is to say, 

$$
\begin{aligned}det[\begin{aligned}⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮ \\ ◻ & ◻ & … & ◻ \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮ \\ △ & △ & … & △ \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮\end{aligned}]=-det[\begin{aligned}⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮ \\ △ & △ & … & △ \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮ \\ ◻ & ◻ & … & ◻ \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f151b612-1bdb-5723-af50-a48439141fbc" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3236 :tutorial/title "Switching Two Rows Changes the Sign of the Determinant"} :step/id #uuid "1889d210-a2bc-5893-b7e3-879d8fc8961f" :step/math-academy-id 17635 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120626}} {:db/id 17592186120704 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121045 :tutorial/content "As we have seen, multiplying a row by a number does not preserve the determinant. However, it does affect the determinant in a predictable way: multiplying a row by a number scales the determinant by that number as well.

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}| & =1\cdot 4-2\cdot 3=-2 \\ |\begin{aligned}2\cdot 1 & 2\cdot 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}|=|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}| & =2\cdot 4-3\cdot 4=-4\end{aligned}
$$

So, in the above example, we have
![](images/08/0826c05fe2eabec96065eb2c83228168129b42c309764df4b101f4a520c4a0f9.svg)

In general, multiplying a row of a matrix by a number multiplies the determinant by that number. That is to say, we can factor out the common multiplier from the row of the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}det[\begin{aligned}⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮ \\ k△ & k△ & … & k△ \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮\end{aligned}]=k\cdot det[\begin{aligned}⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮ \\ △ & △ & … & △ \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "09c28da6-5340-56f9-bbf5-427a824977ee" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3237 :tutorial/title "Multiplying a Row By a Number Scales the Determinant By That Number"} :step/id #uuid "0cc1f27c-f5d8-5b74-9602-32ce4d87b799" :step/math-academy-id 17658 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120627}} {:db/id 17592186120742 :step/content {:db/id 17592186119850 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119665 :question/id #uuid "cbd9b4bc-146a-57f7-a03f-f045f86f3c21" :question/math-academy-id "e-6143"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9a0ab53e-79ff-5520-bb50-069fd381d29d" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120420} {:db/id 17592186120456} {:db/id 17592186265985} {:db/id 17592186265992} {:db/id 17592186265993} {:db/id 17592186265994} {:db/id 17592186329659} {:db/id 17592186329708} {:db/id 17592186378657} {:db/id 17592186383216} {:db/id 17592186385442} {:db/id 17592186409690} {:db/id 17592186411963} {:db/id 17592186424899} {:db/id 17592186483371}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying a Row Operation Given the Connection Between Two Determinants"} :step/id #uuid "e1ec39b0-859a-5c8a-a8ca-f8a0f6371e76" :step/math-academy-id 22905 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120629}} {:db/id 17592186120743 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121061 :tutorial/content "Let's check what happens if we multiply the entire matrix (not only one row) by a number. For example,

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}| & =1\cdot 4-2\cdot 3=-2 \\ |\begin{aligned}3\cdot 1 & 3\cdot 2 \\ 3\cdot 3 & 3\cdot 4\end{aligned}|=|\begin{aligned}3 & 6 \\ 9 & 12\end{aligned}| & =3\cdot 12-6\cdot 9=-18\end{aligned}
$$

So, in the above example, we have

![](images/fe/fe02091dde43a8a2405f6b588f619bc9fa3f54b31ac8a1ac39d318761f00cc3e.svg)

The above is equivalent to multiplying both rows of the matrix by $3$. Multiplying the first row scales the determinant by $3$, and then multiplying the second row scales it by $3$ once more.

In general, multiplying an entire $n \times n$ matrix by a number multiplies the determinant by that number to the power of $n$. That is to say, we can factor out the common multiplier from the entire matrix, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(k\cdot A)={k}^{n}\cdot det(A),\end{aligned}
$$

  I. Swapping two rows

  II. Multiplying a row by a non-zero number

  III. Adding a multiple of one row to another row

Of these three elementary row operations, only III (adding a multiple of one row to another row) *preserves* the determinant. The other two operations, switching two rows or multiplying a row by a non-zero number, *change* the determinant.

To demonstrate, let's consider the matrix ![](images/fa/fa51d7c585db408c47e8640ae839c1a3bbf94e2b0097e1ade511e5773461f1e8.svg) Taking the determinant, we have
![](images/bc/bcf5c5dc9f5b7ed3849e719665f802040cf51e3334ae99e25ea7648cbb0f6134.svg)

If we swap the two rows, we get a different determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}| & =3\cdot 2-1\cdot 4 \\  & =2 \\  & \ne -2\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Likewise, if we multiply top row by ${\color{red}2},$ then we get a different determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2\cdot 1 & 2\cdot 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\cdot 4-3\cdot 4 \\  & =-4 \\  & \ne -2\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

However, if we add twice the top row to the bottom row, then we get the same determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3+2\cdot 1 & 4+2\cdot 2\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 5 & 8\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot 8-2\cdot 5 \\  & =-2\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e5ae8e63-4d2c-5491-9908-96fe94243ab9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3004 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "57d74627-70e0-5830-ba95-6cb026f4de4b" :step/math-academy-id 16213 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120703}} {:db/id 17592186121020 :tutorial/content "Remember the following three standard elementary row operations:

Likewise, if we multiply top row by ${\color{red}2},$ then we get a different determinant:

$$

However, the only difference is the sign of the determinant changes. 

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}| & =1\cdot 4-2\cdot 3=-2 \\ |\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}| & =3\cdot 2-1\cdot 4=2\end{aligned}
$$

So, in the above example, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}| & =-|\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In general, swapping any two rows of a matrix changes the sign of the determinant to the opposite one. That is to say, 

$$
\begin{aligned}det[\begin{aligned}⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮ \\ ◻ & ◻ & … & ◻ \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮ \\ △ & △ & … & △ \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮\end{aligned}]=-det[\begin{aligned}⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮ \\ △ & △ & … & △ \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮ \\ ◻ & ◻ & … & ◻ \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f151b612-1bdb-5723-af50-a48439141fbc" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3236 :tutorial/title "Switching Two Rows Changes the Sign of the Determinant"} :step/id #uuid "1889d210-a2bc-5893-b7e3-879d8fc8961f" :step/math-academy-id 17635 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120626}} {:db/id 17592186120626 :step/content {:db/id 17592186119775 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119589 :question/id #uuid "596aa514-d598-5ffe-affe-f5580d130bd0" :question/math-academy-id "e-4422"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "74764043-e1e7-56d6-8f53-9d287a30e538" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049120}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120452} {:db/id 17592186120454} {:db/id 17592186265957} {:db/id 17592186265958} {:db/id 17592186341848} {:db/id 17592186341849} {:db/id 17592186385422} {:db/id 17592186385557} {:db/id 17592186411964} {:db/id 17592186411965} {:db/id 17592186411967}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Determinant After Switching Two Rows"} :step/id #uuid "07d38f85-837d-577c-a3fa-ed4adb824e28" :step/math-academy-id 16214 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120704}} {:db/id 17592186120704 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121045 :tutorial/content "As we have seen, multiplying a row by a number does not preserve the determinant. However, it does affect the determinant in a predictable way: multiplying a row by a number scales the determinant by that number as well.

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}| & =1\cdot 4-2\cdot 3=-2 \\ |\begin{aligned}2\cdot 1 & 2\cdot 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}|=|\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}| & =2\cdot 4-3\cdot 4=-4\end{aligned}
$$

So, in the above example, we have
![](images/08/0826c05fe2eabec96065eb2c83228168129b42c309764df4b101f4a520c4a0f9.svg)

In general, multiplying a row of a matrix by a number multiplies the determinant by that number. That is to say, we can factor out the common multiplier from the row of the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}det[\begin{aligned}⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮ \\ k△ & k△ & … & k△ \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮\end{aligned}]=k\cdot det[\begin{aligned}⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮ \\ △ & △ & … & △ \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "09c28da6-5340-56f9-bbf5-427a824977ee" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3237 :tutorial/title "Multiplying a Row By a Number Scales the Determinant By That Number"} :step/id #uuid "0cc1f27c-f5d8-5b74-9602-32ce4d87b799" :step/math-academy-id 17658 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120627}} {:db/id 17592186120627 :step/content {:db/id 17592186119776 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119590 :question/id #uuid "89152146-8f04-5b4f-8436-15b82431c35d" :question/math-academy-id "e-4423"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2f11b223-edd2-59b8-b761-164d56e29746" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120453} {:db/id 17592186120455} {:db/id 17592186265963} {:db/id 17592186265964} {:db/id 17592186329660} {:db/id 17592186341851} {:db/id 17592186383167} {:db/id 17592186383174} {:db/id 17592186383181} {:db/id 17592186411968} {:db/id 17592186411969} {:db/id 17592186411970} {:db/id 17592186411971}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Determinant After Multiplying a Row by a Number"} :step/id #uuid "b2bed0ab-d12e-5d90-bbf5-94e480bceb4c" :step/math-academy-id 16215 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120743}} {:db/id 17592186120743 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121061 :tutorial/content "Let's check what happens if we multiply the entire matrix (not only one row) by a number. For example,

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}| & =1\cdot 4-2\cdot 3=-2 \\ |\begin{aligned}3\cdot 1 & 3\cdot 2 \\ 3\cdot 3 & 3\cdot 4\end{aligned}|=|\begin{aligned}3 & 6 \\ 9 & 12\end{aligned}| & =3\cdot 12-6\cdot 9=-18\end{aligned}
$$

So, in the above example, we have

![](images/fe/fe02091dde43a8a2405f6b588f619bc9fa3f54b31ac8a1ac39d318761f00cc3e.svg)

The above is equivalent to multiplying both rows of the matrix by $3$. Multiplying the first row scales the determinant by $3$, and then multiplying the second row scales it by $3$ once more.

In general, multiplying an entire $n \times n$ matrix by a number multiplies the determinant by that number to the power of $n$. That is to say, we can factor out the common multiplier from the entire matrix, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(k\cdot A)={k}^{n}\cdot det(A),\end{aligned}
$$

where $A$ is an $n \times n$ matrix." :tutorial/id #uuid "1c99dfd1-b583-5247-9ac5-c2ada47c0ee9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3880 :tutorial/title "Multiplying a Matrix By a Scalar"} :step/id #uuid "Suppose $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $det(A)=-4.$ What is the value of $det(6A)?$" :question/worked-solution "Multiplying a $n\times n$ matrix by a scalar $k$ is equivalent to multiplying each row by $k,$ and this occurs $n$ times. This leads to the result

$$
\begin{aligned}det(k\cdot A)={k}^{n}\cdot det(A).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have $k=6$ and $n=2.$ Therefore,

$$

- The operation ${R}_{5}↔{R}_{6}$ involves swapping two rows, so it changes the sign of the determinant to the opposite one.

- The operation ${R}_{2}:=\frac{4}{5}{R}_{2}$ involves multiplying a row by $\frac{4}{5},$ so the determinant is multiplied by $\frac{4}{5}$ as well.

Therefore, we have to change the sign of the determinant to the opposite one and multiply by $\frac{4}{5}$ as well. Consequently, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(C) & =\frac{4}{5}\cdot (-det(B)) \\  & =-\frac{4}{5}det(B) \\  & =-\frac{4}{5}\cdot (-75) \\  & =60.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "1776f775-68f2-5dfe-9a78-5fcd889a28cc" :step/next {:db/id 17592186440488}} {:db/id 17592186440488 :step/content {:db/id 17592186383216 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "59b9b5a2-8dd1-5764-aa90-63de7756ab2c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}" :db/id 17592186383218} {:answer/id #uuid "bea9ac5f-6965-5feb-9890-9a84bb8fa9c1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+3{R}_{3}" :db/id 17592186383219} {:answer/id #uuid "c930d2e4-f0f9-5e23-b593-fbc36215932d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+(-3){R}_{3}" :db/id 17592186383220} {:answer/id #uuid "dce12cc1-6fe9-5710-9501-662de6d6ea91" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{R}_{3}:=-3{R}_{3}" :db/id 17592186383221} {:answer/id #uuid "5c5d3036-4719-5fd7-ba58-918a06722081" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{3}" :db/id 17592186383222}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186383220} :answer-field/id #uuid "d2936d46-0370-550d-9d6e-65ba694a9efd" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186383217}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "38a459ba-c9b0-57c4-8ac3-81669bb1022e" :question/math-academy-id "q-130848" :question/problem "Given that $det(A)=det(B),$ which of the following elementary row operations transforms matrix $A$ to matrix $B,$ where

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}0 & -8 & 10 \\ 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}]?
$$" :question/worked-solution "Since $det(A)=det(B)$, the row operation applied to $A$ must be to add or subtract a multiple of one row to another row. In other words, it is of the form 

$$
{R}_{j}:={R}_{j}+(k){R}_{i},\,i\ne j.
$$

By considering the given row operations that are of the above form, we notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}| & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-3){R}_{3} \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & -8 & 10 \\ 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =det(B).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the required row operation is

$$
{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+(-3){R}_{3}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "bc80a516-1dfa-5188-a931-81163ba5b5d8" :step/next {:db/id 17592186440486}} {:db/id 17592186440489 :step/content {:db/id 17592186440484 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "017c23cc-c363-5c6e-87b5-6e7c3ae5e977" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-60" :db/id 17592186440472} {:answer/id #uuid "0d4fda87-7e6e-55cf-a40d-16eb860dbe92" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-75" :db/id 17592186440474} {:answer/id #uuid "81b440ea-43a7-5db4-bd71-d49d81ed4b25" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-30" :db/id 17592186440477} {:answer/id #uuid "b26eabf3-1144-53cd-932b-1525e01f62fe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "90" :db/id 17592186440479} {:answer/id #uuid "fd7979e9-0f01-5714-b611-2b2303ead7b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "75" :db/id 17592186440481}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186440474} :answer-field/id #uuid "e1483cc5-4c9b-5aca-8098-5a910582cb85" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186440483}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ba8abd45-3c22-5be5-a8a7-0f2c616dbcc7" :question/math-academy-id "q-130770" :question/problem "Suppose $Y$ is a $9\times 9$ matrix and $det(Y)=75.$ The matrix $Z$ is obtained from $Y$ by applying the elementary row operations ${R}_{8}↔{R}_{9}$ and ${R}_{7}:={R}_{7}+\frac{2}{5}{R}_{2}.$ What is the value of $det(Z)?$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's figure out what each operation does to the determinant.

:question/math-academy-id "q-130848" :question/problem "Given that $det(A)=det(B),$ which of the following elementary row operations transforms matrix $A$ to matrix $B,$ where

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}0 & -8 & 10 \\ 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}]?
$$" :question/worked-solution "Since $det(A)=det(B)$, the row operation applied to $A$ must be to add or subtract a multiple of one row to another row. In other words, it is of the form 

$$
{R}_{j}:={R}_{j}+(k){R}_{i},\,i\ne j.
$$

By considering the given row operations that are of the above form, we notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}| & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-3){R}_{3} \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & -8 & 10 \\ 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =det(B).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the required row operation is

$$
{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+(-3){R}_{3}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "bc80a516-1dfa-5188-a931-81163ba5b5d8" :step/next {:db/id 17592186440486}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "59b9b5a2-8dd1-5764-aa90-63de7756ab2c" :answer/type {:db/id $$

:step/math-academy-id 33963 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162977}} {:db/id 17592186162974 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163273 :tutorial/content "There are several important properties of the variance of a random variable that we can use to simplify expressions. 

Firstly, the variance of a constant is always zero. That is, for any constant $a,$ we have

$$
\textrm{Var}[a] = 0.
$$

Intuitively, this makes sense. A constant does not vary, so the mean deviation from its expected value should be zero." :tutorial/id #uuid "6eb17ec7-1e57-5d75-8a71-9030a420602b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5458 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "65bbda75-37ec-5809-926a-0fb8d31c008d" :step/math-academy-id 33964 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162971}} {:db/id 17592186162975 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163274 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $X$ is a random variable and $a$ is a constant. Then,

$$
\textrm{Var}[aX] = a^2\textrm{Var}[X].
$$

So, for example, if we know that $\textrm{Var}[X] = 2,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[3X] & ={3}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =9\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =9\cdot 2 \\  & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[-4X] & =(-4)^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =16\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =16\cdot 2 \\  & =32.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** To understand why we have to square the constant when we factor it outside the variance, it's helpful to remember that the variance is defined as the expected *squared* deviation from the mean:

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \textrm E [ (X - \textrm E[X])^2 ]
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[aX] & =\text{E}[(aX-\text{E}[aX])^{2}] \\  & =\text{E}[(aX-a\text{E}[X])^{2}] \\  & =\text{E}[{a}^{2}(X-\text{E}[X])^{2}] \\  & ={a}^{2}\text{E}[(X-\text{E}[X])^{2}] \\  & ={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X].\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "d33b6982-066e-5c82-8138-0283ad8dccbb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5459 :tutorial/title "The Variance of a Scaled Random Variable"} :step/id #uuid "55f9fd86-1f4a-5f2c-b7c2-a60113a4a9e8" :step/math-academy-id 33966 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162972}} {:db/id 17592186162976 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163275 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $X$ is a random variable and $a$ and $b$ are constants. It can be shown that

$$
\textrm{Var}[aX+b] = a^2\textrm{Var}[X].
$$

A proof of this result is given at the end of this lesson.

Therefore, when a random variable is scaled by a factor of $a$ and shifted by a constant $b\mathbin{:}$ 

- the variance is scaled by a factor of $a^2$ as before, and

- the variance is unaffected by the shift.

The fact that shifting a random variable leaves the variance unaltered makes intuitive sense. Shifting all values of $X$ by a fixed amount does not change how far apart those values are from each other. 

For example, if we know that $\textrm{Var}[X] = 3,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[2X+1] & ={2}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & ={2}^{2}\cdot 3 \\  & =4\cdot 3 \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1523e51b-84da-5100-809f-09fbcb0d80ba" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5460 :tutorial/title "The Variance of a Transformed Random Variable"} :step/id #uuid "e17beec2-91ed-5375-9c58-ab279784f2bf" :step/math-academy-id 33968 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162973}} {:db/id 17592186162977 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163276 :tutorial/content "We wish to prove the following result:

$$
\textrm{Var}[aX+b] = a^2\textrm{Var}[X]
$$

Recall that, by definition,

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \textrm E [ (X - \textrm E[X])^2 ].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[aX+b] & =\text{E}[(aX+b-\text{E}[aX+b])^{2}].\end{aligned}
$$

Using the properties of expected value, we can simplify this as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[(aX+b-\text{E}[aX+b])^{2}] & =\text{E}[(aX+b-a\text{E}[X]-b)^{2}] \\  & =\text{E}[(aX-a\text{E}[X])^{2}] \\  & =\text{E}[(a(X-\text{E}[X]))^{2}] \\  & =\text{E}[{a}^{2}(X-\text{E}[X])^{2}] \\  & ={a}^{2}\text{E}[(X-\text{E}[X])^{2}] \\  & ={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X]\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "0372f0de-b6a6-58ee-8195-c04024e8f745" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5461 :tutorial/title "Proof of the General Formula"} :step/id #uuid "da23e59c-3020-5db2-8f5b-77675938bf0b" :step/math-academy-id 33969}] :activity/title "Properties of Variance for Discrete Random Variables" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186162181} {:db/id 17592186162974 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163273 :tutorial/content "There are several important properties of the variance of a random variable that we can use to simplify expressions.

Then,

$$
\textrm{Var}[aX] = a^2\textrm{Var}[X].
$$

So, for example, if we know that $\textrm{Var}[X] = 2,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[3X] & ={3}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =9\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =9\cdot 2 \\  & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[-4X] & =(-4)^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =16\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =16\cdot 2 \\  & =32.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** To understand why we have to square the constant when we factor it outside the variance, it's helpful to remember that the variance is defined as the expected *squared* deviation from the mean:

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \textrm E [ (X - \textrm E[X])^2 ]
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[aX] & =\text{E}[(aX-\text{E}[aX])^{2}] \\  & =\text{E}[(aX-a\text{E}[X])^{2}] \\  & =\text{E}[{a}^{2}(X-\text{E}[X])^{2}] \\  & ={a}^{2}\text{E}[(X-\text{E}[X])^{2}] \\  & ={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X].\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "d33b6982-066e-5c82-8138-0283ad8dccbb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5459 :tutorial/title "The Variance of a Scaled Random Variable"} :step/id #uuid "55f9fd86-1f4a-5f2c-b7c2-a60113a4a9e8" :step/math-academy-id 33966 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162972}} {:db/id 17592186162972 :step/content {:db/id 17592186162057 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161857 :question/id #uuid "a3f88c0e-9426-50d2-baf0-95909e222d4b" :question/math-academy-id "e-9112"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8a3752a0-431d-5520-97b1-493c36bbce54" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186162264} {:db/id 17592186162266} {:db/id 17592186369064} {:db/id 17592186369071} {:db/id 17592186369644} {:db/id 17592186369651} {:db/id 17592186369658} {:db/id 17592186380524} {:db/id 17592186380789} {:db/id 17592186420140} {:db/id 17592186425506} {:db/id 17592186435371} {:db/id 17592186436000} {:db/id 17592186436001}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Variance of a Scaled Random Variable"} :step/id #uuid "fe3d0b73-cb7e-5370-9455-c490da334890" :step/math-academy-id 33961 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162976}} {:db/id 17592186162976 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163275 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $X$ is a random variable and $a$ and $b$ are constants. It can be shown that

$$
\textrm{Var}[aX+b] = a^2\textrm{Var}[X].
$$

A proof of this result is given at the end of this lesson.

Therefore, when a random variable is scaled by a factor of $a$ and shifted by a constant $b\mathbin{:}$ 

- the variance is scaled by a factor of $a^2$ as before, and

- the variance is unaffected by the shift.

The fact that shifting a random variable leaves the variance unaltered makes intuitive sense. Shifting all values of $X$ by a fixed amount does not change how far apart those values are from each other. 

For example, if we know that $\textrm{Var}[X] = 3,$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[2X+1] & ={2}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & ={2}^{2}\cdot 3 \\  & =4\cdot 3 \\  & =12.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Therefore,

$$

Using the properties of expected value, we can simplify this as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[(aX+b-\text{E}[aX+b])^{2}] & =\text{E}[(aX+b-a\text{E}[X]-b)^{2}] \\  & =\text{E}[(aX-a\text{E}[X])^{2}] \\  & =\text{E}[(a(X-\text{E}[X]))^{2}] \\  & =\text{E}[{a}^{2}(X-\text{E}[X])^{2}] \\  & ={a}^{2}\text{E}[(X-\text{E}[X])^{2}] \\  & ={a}^{2}\text{Var}[X]\end{aligned}

Given that $\text{E}[X]=7,$ calculate $\text{Var}[2-5X].$ 

| $x$ | $5$ | $6$ | $9$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $\frac{1}{5}$ | $\frac{2}{5}$ | $\frac{2}{5}$ |" :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "Recall that for any random variable $X$ and constants $a$ and $b,$ we have

$$
\text{Var}[aX+b]={a}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X].
$$

In our case, $a=-5$ and $b=2.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[2-5X] & =(-5)^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =25\cdot \text{Var}[X].\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the variance of $X$ using the following formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Additionally, we're given that $\text{E}[X]=7.$ 

We start by computing $\text{E}[{X}^{2}].$ Summing up the products of each value of ${X}^{2}$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={5}^{2}\cdot f(5)+{6}^{2}\cdot f(6)+{9}^{2}\cdot f(9) \\  & =25(\frac{1}{5})+36(\frac{2}{5})+81(\frac{2}{5}) \\  & =\frac{259}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{259}{5}-{7}^{2} \\  & =\frac{259}{5}-49 \\  & =\frac{14}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[2-5X] & =25\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =25\cdot \frac{14}{5} \\  & =14\cdot 5 \\  & =70.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "1bca5d11-c663-5970-a2d7-41fbabf9a6af" :step/next {:db/id 17592186425509}} {:db/id 17592186425509 :step/content {:db/id 17592186425506 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1ffc334f-bda6-5020-8972-7c141e811580" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "24" :db/id 17592186425494} {:answer/id #uuid "2a01301e-2613-5381-a06c-9e16aa051fd8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186425496} {:answer/id #uuid "3e1bb640-287c-5a4d-9809-a95f12e541cd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{8}{\sqrt{3}}" :db/id 17592186425497} {:answer/id #uuid "559bb6ee-9e3b-59fc-b4ec-1934f445e465" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{8}{3}" :db/id 17592186425498} {:answer/id #uuid "bea01d67-a086-5031-9b05-53086e759f6a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186425502}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186425496} :answer-field/id #uuid "ef907e56-83d3-5832-9059-ba2b6e97be1a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186425504}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "6da9aedf-d051-5c8d-9ea5-b796001b82b1" :question/math-academy-id "q-109056" :question/problem "The probability distribution of the random variable $X$ is given below. | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ |" :question/worked-solution "Recall that for any random variable $X$ and constant $a,$ we have

$$

In our case, $a=\sqrt{3}.$ Therefore,

$$

We can compute the variance of $X$ using the following formula:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}
$$

Additionally, we're given that $\text{E}[X]=2.$ 

We start by computing $\text{E}[{X}^{2}].$ Summing up the products of each value of ${X}^{2}$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={0}^{2}\cdot f(0)+{2}^{2}\cdot f(2)+{4}^{2}\cdot f(4) \\  & =4\cdot \frac{1}{3}+16\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{20}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{20}{3}-{2}^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}

$$

:question/problem "The probability distribution of the random variable $X$ is given below. Given that $\text{E}[X]=0,$ calculate $\text{Var}[\sqrt{5}X+4].$ 

| $x$ | $-1$ | $0$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $\frac{1}{5}$ | $\frac{3}{5}$ | $\frac{1}{5}$ |" :question/worked-solution "Recall that for any random variable $X$ and constants $a$ and $b,$ we have

$$
\text{Var}[aX+b]={a}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X].
$$

In our case, $a=\sqrt{5}$ and $b=4.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\sqrt{5}X+4] & ={(\sqrt{5})}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =5\cdot \text{Var}[X].\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the variance of $X$ using the following formula:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}
$$

Additionally, we're given that $\text{E}[X]=0.$ 

We start by computing $\text{E}[{X}^{2}].$ Summing up the products of each value of ${X}^{2}$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & =(-1)^{2}\cdot f(-1)+{0}^{2}\cdot f(0)+{1}^{2}\cdot f(1) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{5} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}-{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\sqrt{5}X+4] & =5\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =5\cdot \frac{2}{5} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "02fca583-999d-5fea-95bb-2fa89ae7e5ac" :step/next {:db/id 17592186435374}} {:db/id 17592186435373 :step/content {:db/id 17592186435371 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "039f84c9-15b6-5535-9aa7-17f63520b5ea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186435365} {:answer/id #uuid "31713117-0676-52eb-93ae-63c695655871" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186435366} {:answer/id #uuid "7d294bd2-f457-5854-b801-d01d068966a4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186435367} {:answer/id #uuid "a9534937-1eca-5636-899b-550bfbfe6e07" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{8}" :db/id 17592186435368} {:answer/id #uuid "fc28d66e-a0b9-5d76-9c20-a4f103450187" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186435369}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186435367} :answer-field/id #uuid "aadf43d0-7c01-553a-93ba-140bd9fcc568" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186435370}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "a7e780b8-35dc-5693-8651-c458793347c5" :question/math-academy-id "q-109059" :question/problem "The probability distribution of the random variable $X$ is given below. | $f(x)$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{5}{8}$ |" :question/worked-solution "Recall that for any random variable $X$ and constant $a,$ we have

$$
\text{Var}[aX]={a}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X].
$$

In our case, $a=\frac{1}{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\frac{1}{2}X] & ={(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \text{Var}[X].\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the variance of $X$ using the following formula:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}
$$

Additionally, we're given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{9}{2}.$ 

We start by computing $\text{E}[{X}^{2}].$ Summing up the products of each value of ${X}^{2}$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={0}^{2}\cdot f(0)+{3}^{2}\cdot f(3)+{6}^{2}\cdot f(6) \\  & =9\cdot \frac{1}{4}+36\cdot \frac{5}{8} \\  & =\frac{99}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{99}{4}-{(\frac{9}{2})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\frac{1}{2}X] & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{9}{2} \\  & =\frac{9}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "b23b860b-4012-51e9-9c6f-d158c0177636" :step/next {:db/id 17592186436006}} {:db/id 17592186436006 :step/content {:db/id 17592186420139 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3dcfce52-9f77-594e-abb6-a96da80d166b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.2" :db/id 17592186420112} {:answer/id #uuid "5dae0172-10cc-5060-bf4a-315f77dba9a3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186420115} {:answer/id #uuid "6657c628-8660-5023-8ee0-945dab5715e8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186420117} {:answer/id #uuid "95c4162c-b36b-54af-9f0c-c093bb7cac5f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.1" :db/id 17592186420119} {:answer/id #uuid "e3fddd96-3d89-5025-83fd-0275af9c34a1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186420126}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186420126} :answer-field/id #uuid "53761adc-2f46-5607-b9dd-4ae8e7e441a8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186420133}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "64dd6f3a-caa4-5c03-ba3a-d02448881df5" :question/math-academy-id "q-129381" :question/problem "$\text{Var}[0.2]=$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that for any constant $a,$ we have

$$

{:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "eff26da6-299d-5b1f-93b8-02b4dbf809cb" :question/math-academy-id "q-109064" :question/problem "The probability distribution of the random variable $X$ is given below. Given that $\text{E}[X]=3,$ calculate $\text{Var}[7X].$ 

| $x$ | $1$ | $2$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $\frac{1}{7}$ | $\frac{2}{7}$ | $\frac{4}{7}$ |" :question/worked-solution "Recall that for any random variable $X$ and constant $a,$ we have

$$
\text{Var}[aX]={a}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X].
$$

In our case, $a=7.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[7X] & ={7}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =49\cdot \text{Var}[X].\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the variance of $X$ using the following formula:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}
$$

Additionally, we're given that $\text{E}[X]=3.$ 

We start by computing $\text{E}[{X}^{2}].$ Summing up the products of each value of ${X}^{2}$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={1}^{2}\cdot f(1)+{2}^{2}\cdot f(2)+{4}^{2}\cdot f(4) \\  & =1\cdot \frac{1}{7}+4\cdot \frac{2}{7}+16\cdot \frac{4}{7} \\  & =\frac{73}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{73}{7}-{3}^{2} \\  & =\frac{10}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[7X] & =49\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =49\cdot \frac{10}{7} \\  & =70.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "de016c0c-5fd8-5def-85ac-87352e4b87f8" :step/next {:db/id 17592186436005}} {:db/id 17592186436004 :step/content {:db/id 17592186436002 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "34fbef3e-ce0c-5e42-8083-bb856bed6a54" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186435977} {:answer/id #uuid "87337578-c732-5754-be09-02283229f965" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "23" :db/id 17592186435982} {:answer/id #uuid "9b8996e1-6f9f-5075-9e74-0c9956ec327f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "20" :db/id 17592186435983} {:answer/id #uuid "cad3e623-6a5f-55d5-841b-565c29e0e0bb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186435988} {:answer/id #uuid "d315913a-19d5-543a-b877-666f53b9143f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186435990}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186435988} :answer-field/id #uuid "abd7ad31-b561-5286-91ce-40ec287b64f1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186435997}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "f691affc-d374-513b-ace4-47b0fed08cd8" :question/math-academy-id "q-129394" :question/problem "If $\text{Var}[X]=100,$ calculate $\text{Var}[3-0.2X].$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that for any random variable $X$ and constants $a$ and $b,$ we have

| $x$ | $0$ | $3$ | $6$ |

$$
\text{Var}[aX]={a}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X].
$$

In our case, $a=\frac{1}{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\frac{1}{2}X] & ={(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \text{Var}[X].\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the variance of $X$ using the following formula:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}
$$

Additionally, we're given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{9}{2}.$ 

We start by computing $\text{E}[{X}^{2}].$ Summing up the products of each value of ${X}^{2}$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={0}^{2}\cdot f(0)+{3}^{2}\cdot f(3)+{6}^{2}\cdot f(6) \\  & =9\cdot \frac{1}{4}+36\cdot \frac{5}{8} \\  & =\frac{99}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{99}{4}-{(\frac{9}{2})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[\frac{1}{2}X] & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \text{Var}[X] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{9}{2} \\  & =\frac{9}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "b23b860b-4012-51e9-9c6f-d158c0177636" :step/next {:db/id 17592186436006}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "771854e8-d892-5203-a97d-09439ca5fe0b" :answer/type {:db/id :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186116133 :step/content {:db/id 17592186116498 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find the inverse of the matrix 

![](images/fd/fd9e9dc44e27810ef490a898a7c82ae9296eaf85ac9406cf310afe86638f71e1.svg) 

We can compute the inverse of $A$ using elementary row operations. There are two key advantages to using row operations to compute the inverse of a matrix:

- The method works for any invertible matrix of any size, not just $2\times 2$ matrices.

- It requires significantly less computation than some alternative methods. This is especially true for large matrices.

Here, we'll focus on the $2\times 2$ case. We use the following fact:

*The row operations that transform $A$ into the identity matrix $I_2$ also transform $I_2$ into $A^{-1}$*.

So, to find the inverse of $A,$ we proceed as follows:

**Step 1:** Write down $\color{blue}A$ and the identity matrix $I_2$ side-by-side, as shown below:
![](images/e5/e553bcc265698432452c8d35b79fe9dc70c25010a0bcc6874ad0302ea7033ed7.svg)

**Step 2:** Apply the standard Gauss-Jordan method to transform the matrix $A$ into the identity matrix. We perform the same row operations on both matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}[A\,|\,{I}_{2}\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 7 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 7 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\,I\,|\,{A}^{-1}]\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix $A^{-1}$ is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore, 

![](images/b7/b7c08e9a28ebfe456a9d77ccdaf6688893dfd04ba755a989a417c8a43e80ee0c.svg)

We can easily check our result by computing $AA^{-1}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}A{A}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}7 & -2 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "fc38ae42-2cd4-53df-9ad5-568d8e3b5fd4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3167 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "d8efc5ed-eaaf-514d-b03a-248df406a7d5" :step/math-academy-id ![](images/fd/fd9e9dc44e27810ef490a898a7c82ae9296eaf85ac9406cf310afe86638f71e1.svg) 

We can compute the inverse of $A$ using elementary row operations. There are two key advantages to using row operations to compute the inverse of a matrix:

- The method works for any invertible matrix of any size, not just $2\times 2$ matrices.

- It requires significantly less computation than some alternative methods. This is especially true for large matrices.

Here, we'll focus on the $2\times 2$ case. We use the following fact:

*The row operations that transform $A$ into the identity matrix $I_2$ also transform $I_2$ into $A^{-1}$*.

So, to find the inverse of $A,$ we proceed as follows:

**Step 1:** Write down $\color{blue}A$ and the identity matrix $I_2$ side-by-side, as shown below:
![](images/e5/e553bcc265698432452c8d35b79fe9dc70c25010a0bcc6874ad0302ea7033ed7.svg)

**Step 2:** Apply the standard Gauss-Jordan method to transform the matrix $A$ into the identity matrix. We perform the same row operations on both matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}[A\,|\,{I}_{2}\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 7 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 7 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\,I\,|\,{A}^{-1}]\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix $A^{-1}$ is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore, 

![](images/b7/b7c08e9a28ebfe456a9d77ccdaf6688893dfd04ba755a989a417c8a43e80ee0c.svg)

We can easily check our result by computing $AA^{-1}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}A{A}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}7 & -2 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "fc38ae42-2cd4-53df-9ad5-568d8e3b5fd4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3167 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "d8efc5ed-eaaf-514d-b03a-248df406a7d5" :step/math-academy-id 17230 :step/next {:db/id 17592186116136}} {:db/id 17592186116498 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find the inverse of the matrix

Unbounded Interval"} :step/id #uuid "61e344b0-9976-54f7-a03c-175fe1505fbb" :step/math-academy-id 27841} {:db/id 17592186158167 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158491 :tutorial/content "A **Poisson distribution** is a probability distribution that models the number of events that occur in an interval of time or space if events occur independently and at a constant average rate.

If the rate of the events is $\lambda,$ then the number of events $x$ occurring in an interval of fixed length has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{\lambda^x e^{-\lambda}}{x!}, \qquad x=0,1,2,3, \ldots
$$

If a random variable $X$ follows a Poisson distribution with rate $\lambda,$ then we write $X \sim \textrm{Po}(\lambda).$

For example, suppose that calls come in at an average rate of $3$ calls per minute at a call center. Then the number of calls $X$ that are received during the next minute has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{3^x e^{-3}}{x!}
$$

In particular, the probability of receiving $4$ calls during the next minute is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=4) & =f(4) \\  & =\frac{{3}^{4}{e}^{-3}}{4!} \\  & ≈0.168\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places." :tutorial/id #uuid "6e07ef85-f3ca-52c8-89e2-062d8ea7c9eb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4525 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "fd4dd871-25f7-54f5-9345-a556f2356cb0" :step/math-academy-id 27850 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158170}} {:db/id 17592186158170 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158493 :tutorial/content "The shape of the graph of the Poisson distribution depends on the value of $\lambda.$ When $\lambda$ is small, the probability is concentrated at small values of $x.$ When $\lambda$ is larger, the probability is concentrated at larger values of $x.$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

You may assume that rental requests occur independently and at a constant average rate." :question/worked-solution "A Poisson random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda $ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{\lambda }^{x}{e}^{-\lambda }}{x!}
$$

Let $X$ be the number of cars rented in a day. Since the average rate is $3$ requests per day, and events occur independently and at a constant average rate, the number of rented cars can be modeled as a Poisson random variable with rate $\lambda =3,$ and we can write $X∼\text{Po}(3).$

So, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{3}^{x}{e}^{-3}}{x!}
$$

Therefore, the probability that none of the cars are rented the next day is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=0) & =f(0) \\  & =\frac{{3}^{0}{e}^{-3}}{0!} \\  & ≈0.050\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places."} :step/id #uuid "f54fa653-ea98-5ece-9516-abf27f41ad60" :step/next {:db/id 17592186437142}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid $$

Let $X$ be the number of bacteria in one milliliter of the liquid. Since the average rate is $6$ bacteria per milliliter, and events occur independently and at a constant average rate, the number of bacteria can be modeled as a Poisson random variable with rate $\lambda =6,$ and we can write $X∼\text{Po}(6).$

$$
f(x)=\frac{{6}^{x}{e}^{-6}}{x!}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 3) & =P(X\in \{0,1,2,3\}) \\  & =f(0)+f(1)+f(2)+f(3) \\  & =\frac{{6}^{0}{e}^{-6}}{0!}+\frac{{6}^{1}{e}^{-6}}{1!}+\frac{{6}^{2}{e}^{-6}}{2!}+\frac{{6}^{3}{e}^{-6}}{3!} \\  & ≈0.151\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places."} :step/id #uuid "a6a9e584-e23b-5f27-aa56-050dc0d31fff" :step/next {:db/id 17592186437143}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid You may assume that defective transistors occur independently and at a constant average rate." :question/worked-solution "A Poisson random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda $ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{\lambda }^{x}{e}^{-\lambda }}{x!}
$$

Let $X$ be the number of defective transistors in a batch of transistors. Since the average rate is $1$ defective transistors per batch, and events occur independently and at a constant average rate, the number of defective transistors can be modeled as a Poisson random variable with rate $\lambda =1,$ and we can write $X∼\text{Po}(1).$

So, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{1}^{x}{e}^{-1}}{x!}
$$

Therefore, the probability that in the next batch of transistors, there will be less than $4$ defective transistors is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<4) & =P(X\in \{0,1,2,3\}) \\  & =f(0)+f(1)+f(2)+f(3) \\  & =\frac{{1}^{0}{e}^{-1}}{0!}+\frac{{1}^{1}{e}^{-1}}{1!}+\frac{{1}^{2}{e}^{-1}}{2!}+\frac{{1}^{3}{e}^{-1}}{3!} \\  & ≈0.981\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places."} :step/id #uuid "db7e6473-de0a-51cd-a4c0-7c7adca3341e"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "16527557-36e3-5765-85fe-85ad503bd10f" :answer/type {:db/id :topic/id #uuid "f5218ca7-a9d3-5ad9-b17a-ee16b6e2b34a" :topic/math-academy-id 1805} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186120711 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121049 :tutorial/content "Suppose we know that a plane $\Pi$ passes through the point $P(1,1,2)$ and that the vector $\mathbf{n}=\langle 0,0,3 \rangle$ is perpendicular to the plane. Let's write down an equation of this plane using the dot product.

![](images/0f/0f8353480099369ad92701d1799f72d46eab4bbe5c17add8cb37a4f34074311b.png)

We start by considering an arbitrary point $R(x,y,z)$ that lies on the plane. The position vectors of the points $R$ and $P$ are $\mathbf{r}=\langle x,y,z \rangle$ and $\mathbf{p}=\langle 1,1,2 \rangle$ respectively. So, the vector

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PR} & =r-p \\  & =r-⟨1,1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

is parallel to the plane. Therefore, $\overrightarrow{PR} \perp \mathbf{n},$ as shown below.

![](images/28/28b6770bd681257b1030679a421b80e3f3d1e8fbb86d2060b64c7301d0878c5c.png)

Now, recall that if two nonzero vectors are perpendicular, then their dot product is zero:

$$
\overrightarrow{PR}\perp \mathbf{n} \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \overrightarrow{PR}\cdot \mathbf{n} = 0
$$

So, we get the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is called the **vector equation of the plane** that passes through the point $P(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ and is perpendicular to the vector $\mathbf{n}.$ In our case, we obtain

$$
(\mathbf{r} - \langle 1,1,2 \rangle) \cdot \langle 0,0,3 \rangle = 0.
$$

**Note:** Using the properties of the dot product, we can arrive at an alternative vector equation given by

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n-p\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot n & =c\end{aligned}
$$

where $c = \mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{n}$ is a (scalar) constant." :tutorial/id #uuid "77d83d72-9202-50d7-af28-72062f00bfa5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3255 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "1b13bc4d-57be-5d17-841a-4f2645bc3982" :step/math-academy-id 17921} {:db/id 17592186120870 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121120 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a plane with the following normal vector: 

$$
\mathbf{n}=\langle -1,2,1 \rangle
$$

Let's use the scalar product to find a vector that is parallel to this plane.

We denote our parallel vector as $\mathbf{v} = \langle t_1,t_2,t_3 \rangle.$ Now, since $\mathbf{v} \perp \mathbf{n},$ we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}v\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨{t}_{1},{t}_{2},{t}_{3}⟩\cdot ⟨-1,2,1⟩ & =0 \\ -{t}_{1}+2{t}_{2}+{t}_{3} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We now need to find a nonzero solution to this equation. To do that, we solve the equation for *one* of the variables (it doesn't matter which one). For example, let's solve our equation for the variable $t_1\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}_{1} & =2{t}_{2}+{t}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Here, the variable $t_1$ depends on $t_2$ and $t_3,$ which, in turn, can be *any* real numbers. The variables $t_2$ and $t_3$ are called **free variables**.

Hence, the general form of our vector $\mathbf{v}$ is

$$
\mathbf{v}=\langle 2t_2+t_3, \, t_2, \, t_3 \rangle,
$$

where $t_2, t_3 \in (-\infty,\infty).$

To find a particular vector parallel to the plane, we can substitute any values for $t_2$ and $t_3\mathbin{:}$

- For example, setting $t_2=0$ and $t_3=1$, we get

$$
\mathbf{v}_1= \langle 1, 0, 1 \rangle.
$$

- Or, we could set $t_2=1$ and $t_3=0$ and get

$$
\mathbf{v}_2 = \langle 2, 1, 0 \rangle.
$$

**Note:** There are infinitely many vectors parallel to a given plane. In our example, we found only two particular vectors." :tutorial/id #uuid "980ef6f4-542d-5915-84b8-e34f4480ae68" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6411 :tutorial/title "A Vector Parallel To a Plane"} :step/id #uuid "69d22458-d2d5-5c3d-b6fb-4714f2ea1b49" :step/math-academy-id 38733 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120713}}] :activity/title "The Vector Equation of a Plane" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186120016} {:db/id 17592186120711 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121049 :tutorial/content "Suppose we know that a plane $\Pi$ passes through the point $P(1,1,2)$ and that the vector $\mathbf{n}=\langle 0,0,3 \rangle$ is perpendicular to the plane. Let's write down an equation of this plane using the dot product.

![](images/0f/0f8353480099369ad92701d1799f72d46eab4bbe5c17add8cb37a4f34074311b.png)

We start by considering an arbitrary point $R(x,y,z)$ that lies on the plane. The position vectors of the points $R$ and $P$ are $\mathbf{r}=\langle x,y,z \rangle$ and $\mathbf{p}=\langle 1,1,2 \rangle$ respectively. So, the vector

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PR} & =r-p \\  & =r-⟨1,1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

is parallel to the plane. Therefore, $\overrightarrow{PR} \perp \mathbf{n},$ as shown below.

![](images/28/28b6770bd681257b1030679a421b80e3f3d1e8fbb86d2060b64c7301d0878c5c.png)

Now, recall that if two nonzero vectors are perpendicular, then their dot product is zero:

$$
\overrightarrow{PR}\perp \mathbf{n} \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \overrightarrow{PR}\cdot \mathbf{n} = 0
$$

So, we get the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is called the **vector equation of the plane** that passes through the point $P(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ and is perpendicular to the vector $\mathbf{n}.$ In our case, we obtain

$$
(\mathbf{r} - \langle 1,1,2 \rangle) \cdot \langle 0,0,3 \rangle = 0.
$$

**Note:** Using the properties of the dot product, we can arrive at an alternative vector equation given by

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n-p\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot n & =c\end{aligned}
$$

where $c = \mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{n}$ is a (scalar) constant." :tutorial/id #uuid "77d83d72-9202-50d7-af28-72062f00bfa5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3255 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "cf165cc4-ae6c-564d-b8e6-051c7aba1faa" :step/math-academy-id 17917 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120712}} {:db/id 17592186121049 :tutorial/content "Suppose we know that a plane $\Pi$ passes through the point $P(1,1,2)$ and that the vector $\mathbf{n}=\langle 0,0,3 \rangle$ is perpendicular to the plane. ![](images/28/28b6770bd681257b1030679a421b80e3f3d1e8fbb86d2060b64c7301d0878c5c.png)

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=2-3t \\ y=3+4t \\ z=4-t.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Note that the position vector of $P$ is $p=⟨3,-5,-2⟩.$ Converting the parametric equations of the line to vector form, we get

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=2-3t \\ y=3+4t \\ z=4-t\end{aligned}\,⟹\,⟨x,y,z⟩=⟨2,3,4⟩+t\text{ }{{⟨-3,4,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{v}.
$$

 

The direction vector of the line is $v=⟨-3,4,-1⟩,$ so a normal vector to the plane is 

$$
n=v=⟨-3,4,-1⟩.
$$

Therefore, the equation of the plane is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n-p\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨-3,4,-1⟩ & =⟨3,-5,-2⟩\cdot ⟨-3,4,-1⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨-3,4,-1⟩ & =-27.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "6262b847-bfad-5541-b7d9-0c48d99eb024" :step/next {:db/id 17592186420155}} {:db/id 17592186420155 :step/content {:db/id 17592186262846 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1066db60-12af-5e82-a7c0-d24afa450e35" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{7}" :db/id 17592186260024} {:answer/id #uuid "336d23d9-d848-54ca-86e6-782c1b13a369" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186260339} {:answer/id #uuid "6bfd83ea-5bb5-57e7-b814-e0e365ce1b44" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3" :db/id 17592186260820} {:answer/id #uuid "d4093fa7-7b24-5445-bf63-718de7a82e0c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186261744} {:answer/id #uuid "f03309e1-ca15-5335-aab5-a2535a4337a6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186261981}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186260339} :answer-field/id #uuid "f46674a6-7e2b-5656-b018-7f5bf5e7afa0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186262547}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "aa3bed00-1af4-5c46-8c12-264209634c51" :question/math-academy-id "q-127910" :question/problem "A nonzero vector $⟨a,\,0,\,c⟩$ is parallel to the plane $r\cdot ⟨-1,1,3⟩=\sqrt{7}.$ What is the value of $\frac{a}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "We need a vector $v=⟨{t}_{1},{t}_{2},{t}_{3}⟩$ that is parallel to the given plane. 

From the equation $r\cdot ⟨-1,1,3⟩=\sqrt{7}$ of the plane, we get the normal vector $n=⟨-1,1,3⟩.$ So, $v⊥n$ and we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}v\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨{t}_{1},{t}_{2},{t}_{3}⟩\cdot ⟨-1,1,3⟩ & =0 \\ -{t}_{1}+{t}_{2}+3{t}_{3} & =0 \\ {t}_{1} & ={t}_{2}+3{t}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we obtain 

$$
v=⟨{t}_{2}+3{t}_{3},\,{t}_{2},{t}_{3}⟩,
$$

where ${t}_{2},{t}_{3}\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ 

We are told that the second component of $v$ equals $0.$ So, we must set ${t}_{2}=0.$ 

Since $v$ is nonzero, we can pick any ${t}_{3}\ne 0.$ For example, setting ${t}_{3}=1$, we get

$$
v=⟨3,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Therefore, $\frac{a}{c}=3.$"} :step/id #uuid "6f1edd60-137c-5af0-bf08-f3f3e9df0344" :step/next {:db/id 17592186420156}} {:db/id 17592186420156 :step/content {:db/id 17592186420153 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1b182a09-cc9d-51c4-95fe-e78790ecf72a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186420142} {:answer/id #uuid "36cb63bc-ae79-51e4-b5ab-3039c42340e0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186420143} {:answer/id #uuid "4173b538-e381-5dd5-b0c5-10dc2eaa96c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{3}" :db/id 17592186420144} {:answer/id #uuid "502b671f-b1be-5d29-8f96-08571a87d173" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186420145} {:answer/id #uuid "72001519-6957-56f0-b511-f27a9ed3c85f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}" :db/id 17592186420146}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186420143} :answer-field/id #uuid "f9a0d8dd-871f-5fc8-9699-7a78c5f80aac" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186420152}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "3fa29ff6-5ae4-5642-82fd-03b1645e810c" :question/math-academy-id "q-127921" :question/problem "A nonzero vector $⟨0,\,b,\,c⟩$ is parallel to the plane $r\cdot ⟨5,-1,3⟩=27.$ What is the value of $\frac{b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "We need a vector $v=⟨{t}_{1},{t}_{2},{t}_{3}⟩$ that is parallel to the given plane. 

From the equation $r\cdot ⟨5,-1,3⟩=27$ of the plane, we get the normal vector $n=⟨5,-1,3⟩.$ So, $v⊥n$ and we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}v\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨{t}_{1},{t}_{2},{t}_{3}⟩\cdot ⟨5,-1,3⟩ & =0 \\ 5{t}_{1}-{t}_{2}+3{t}_{3} & =0 \\ {t}_{2} & =5{t}_{1}+3{t}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
