Variables Are Negative"}] :question/problem "Simplify $\sqrt{y^4 z^{6}}$ given that $z \lt 0$." :question/worked-solution "The square root of a squared quantity can be simplified using absolute value.

$$
\sqrt{x^2} = \mid x \mid
$$

In our case, we can simplify the given expression as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned} \sqrt{y^4 z^{6}} \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{y^2 z^3 \cdot y^2 z^3} \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{\left(y^2 z^3\right)^2} \\[5pt] &= \begin{vmatrix}y^2 z^3 & \\[5pt] &= & y^2 & \cdot & z^3 & \\[5pt] &= & y^2 & \cdot\left.\end{vmatrix}z\right|^3 \end{aligned}
$$

A squared number is always positive or zero, and the absolute value of any positive (or zero) number is itself, so we have

$$
\mid y^2 \mid = y^2
$$

On the other hand, we are told that $z \lt 0$, and to take the absolute value of any negative number we need to flip the sign, so we have

$$
\mid z \mid = -z
$$

Therefore, our final answer is

$$
\begin{vmatrix}y^{2} & \cdot\left.\end{vmatrix}z\right|^{3} = y^{2} \cdot (-z)^{3} =-y^{2}z^{3}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186179915 :question/id #uuid "5ed8c3c3-e99d-5562-af54-3cfe4307c231" :question/math-academy-id "q-110917"} {:db/id 17592186180213 :question/id #uuid "4c2c0434-5859-5978-aab5-e68699fd391c" :question/math-academy-id "q-52301"} {:db/id 17592186179762 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179462 :question/id #uuid "4b7c6339-6e9c-5047-a95f-3daf41db4a8a" :question/math-academy-id "e-1353"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5b8f0a91-f0de-5907-9c96-eac8a3a0e7cf" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049636} {:db/id 17592186049843}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180161 :question/id #uuid "ec502873-fbf5-5e68-afb5-0d5690849cc7" :question/math-academy-id "q-2930"} {:db/id 17592186180216 :question/id #uuid "4a6883eb-bb60-5def-b4e7-f188c803a578" :question/math-academy-id "q-52510"}] :knowledge-point/title "Simplifying an Expression Given That Some Variables Are Non-Negative"} {:db/id 17592186179462 :question/id #uuid "4b7c6339-6e9c-5047-a95f-3daf41db4a8a" :question/math-academy-id "e-1353" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186179762 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5b8f0a91-f0de-5907-9c96-eac8a3a0e7cf" :knowledge-point/title "Simplifying an Expression Given That Some Variables Are Non-Negative"}] :question/problem "Simplify $\sqrt{\dfrac{r^2}{s^2}}$ given that $s>0$." :question/worked-solution "The square root of a squared quantity can be simplified using absolute value:

$$
\sqrt{x^2} = \mid x \mid
$$

In our case, we can simplify the given expression as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned} \sqrt{\dfrac{r^2}{s^2}} \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{\dfrac{r}{s} \cdot \dfrac{r}{s}} \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{r}{s}\right)^2} \\[5pt] &= \left|\dfrac{r}{s}\right| \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\begin{vmatrix}r &}{\mid s\end{vmatrix}} & \end{aligned}
$$

We are told that $s \gt 0$, and we know that the absolute value of any positive number is just itself, so we have

$$
\mid s \mid = s
$$

Therefore, our final answer is

$$
\dfrac{\begin{vmatrix}r &}{\begin{vmatrix}s &} = \dfrac{\end{vmatrix}r\end{vmatrix}}{s}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049636} {:db/id 17592186049843} {:db/id 17592186180161 :question/id #uuid "ec502873-fbf5-5e68-afb5-0d5690849cc7" :question/math-academy-id "q-2930" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186180517 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180733 :tutorial/content "The square root of a squared quantity can be simplified using absolute value.

$$
\sqrt{x^2} = \mid x \mid
$$

However, if the domain of the variable is restricted, some expressions might allow further simplification.

For example, suppose we know that $a>0$. Let's use this information to fully simplify $\sqrt{36a^2}$.

We can start by simplifying the expression as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{36a^{2}} &=  \\
\sqrt{(6a)^{2}} &=  \\
\mid 6a \mid &=  \\
&= \begin{vmatrix}6 & \cdot & a\end{vmatrix} \\
&= 6 \mid a \mid
\end{aligned}
$$

We are told that $a>0$, and we know that the absolute value of any positive number is just itself, so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mid a &= a
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our final answer is

$$
6 \mid a \mid = 6a
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "414812ea-abcc-59df-98fa-8a79ae36a1a5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5905 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c8a28231-be54-56e8-b63b-3e1a42d1360e" :step/math-academy-id 36113 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180548}} {:db/id 17592186180521 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180736 :tutorial/content "Let's see what changes if we consider square roots of perfect squares when some variables are negative.

For example, suppose that $t \lt 0$. Let's use this to simplify the expression $\sqrt{t^2}$.

Simplifying this expression in the usual way, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} \sqrt{t^2} \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{(t)^2} \\[5pt] &= \mid t \mid.& \end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $t \lt 0$. To take the absolute value of a negative number, we need to flip the sign. This gives

$$
\mid t \mid = -t
$$

Therefore, our final answer is

$$
{\color{blue}\sqrt{t^2}} = {\color{red}-t}
$$

You can convince yourself that this is correct by plugging a few values of $t$ into the above equation. Provided that $t$ is negative, this expression will always give a true statement.

For example, suppose that $t = -2$. Substituting into the left-hand side of the equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{t^{2}} &=  \\
\sqrt{(-2)^{2}} &=  \\
\sqrt{4} &=  \\
&= 2 \mid
\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $t=-2$ into the right-hand side of the equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
-t &=  \\
- (-2) &=  \\
&= 2 \mid
\end{aligned}
$$

Since both sides give the same result, the statement is true." :tutorial/id #uuid "1f0207ef-9d6a-584b-8d44-a92c732cce4b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5928 :tutorial/title "The Square Root of a Perfect Square With Negative Variables"} :step/id #uuid "8e668d2a-9da1-5eaf-be19-c24fd0a3b12a" :step/math-academy-id 36179 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180547}} {:db/id 17592186180547 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179761 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179461 :question/id #uuid "27032e03-f6b6-5f66-b514-d3b9c4f79ec0" :question/math-academy-id "e-1352"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a7d2284f-c4ba-571f-91a6-be472f185c0b" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186179915} {:db/id 17592186180213}] :knowledge-point/title "Simplifying an Expression Given That Some Variables Are Negative"} :step/id #uuid "9a309239-eefc-54be-8199-bbf772d5350e" :step/math-academy-id 4285} {:db/id 17592186180548 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179762 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179462 :question/id #uuid "4b7c6339-6e9c-5047-a95f-3daf41db4a8a" :question/math-academy-id "e-1353"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5b8f0a91-f0de-5907-9c96-eac8a3a0e7cf" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049636} {:db/id 17592186049843}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180161} {:db/id 17592186180216}] :knowledge-point/title "Simplifying an Expression Given That Some Variables Are Non-Negative"} :step/id #uuid "35d16b06-b444-5257-a405-5223a9834174" :step/math-academy-id 4287 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180521}}] :activity/title "The Square Root of a Perfect Square With Domain Restrictions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186179879} {:db/id 17592186180517 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180733 :tutorial/content "The square root of a squared quantity can be simplified using absolute value.

$$
\mid t \mid = -t
$$

Therefore, our final answer is

$$
{\color{blue}\sqrt{t^2}} = {\color{red}-t}
$$

You can convince yourself that this is correct by plugging a few values of $t$ into the above equation. Provided that $t$ is negative, this expression will always give a true statement.

For example, suppose that $t = -2$. Substituting into the left-hand side of the equation, we get

$$

\sqrt{(-2)^{2}} &=  \\
\sqrt{4} &=  \\
&= 2 \mid
\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $t=-2$ into the right-hand side of the equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
-t &=  \\
- (-2) &=  \\
&= 2 \mid
\end{aligned}
$$

B={[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5\end{aligned}]},\,[T]_{B|C}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ (shown above) and a basis $C$ of ${R}^{3}.$
The matrix $[T]_{B|C}$ of the linear map $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{3}$ relative to these bases, and the vector $x\in {R}^{2},$ are also given. Find $[T(x)]_{C}.$" :question/worked-solution "We can find the coordinates of the image of $x$ under $T$ relative to the basis $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[T(x)]_{C} & =[T]_{B|C}\cdot [x]_{B}\end{aligned}
$$

First, we need to find $[x]_{B},$ the coordinates of $x$ relative to $B.$ So, let

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ -3\end{aligned}]={x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$

This gives us the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}=-4 \\ -2{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=-3.\end{aligned}
$$

We now row-reduce the corresponding augmented matrix using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & -4 \\ -2 & 5 & -3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 4 \\ -2 & 5 & -3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 5 & 5\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:=\frac{1}{5}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Finally, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}[T(x)]_{C} & =[T]_{B|C}\cdot [x]_{B} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 5 \\ 10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186392205 :question/id #uuid "b03e0038-023a-5069-84d1-998d6d535a68" :question/math-academy-id "q-38540"} {:db/id 17592186395295 :question/id #uuid [{:db/id 17592186125440 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125799 :tutorial/content "Let's suppose we have the linear map

$$
\mathbf T: {\color{blue}V} \to {\color{red}W}
$$

where the bases of the vector spaces $\color{blue}V$ and ${\color{red}W}$ respectively are given by

$$
{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}=\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{b}_1},{\color{blue}\mathbf{b}_2}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{b}_3} \}, \qquad \qquad {\color{red}\mathcal{C}} = \{ {\color{red}\mathbf{c}_1},{\color{red}\mathbf{c}_2} \}.
$$

The **matrix of $\mathbf{T}$ with respect to the bases $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ and $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$** is the matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors $\mathbf{T}({\color{blue}\mathbf{b}_1}),$ $\mathbf{T}(\color{blue}{\mathbf{b}_2}),$ and $\mathbf{T}({\color{blue}\mathbf{b}_3})$ relative to the basis ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{B|C} & =[\begin{aligned}| & | & | \\ [T({b}_{1})]_{C} & [T({b}_{2})]_{C} & [T({b}_{3})]_{C} \\ | & | & |\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

For example, if 

![](images/be/be8cff88ef83ebc67d0df7a50a243c55c8f11aa92e7a07f64b73bb30ed701392.svg)

then

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{B|C} & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 10 & -12 \\ 1 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "da91373e-0973-56a4-91c9-aa2a2b1de0b1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3589 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "9ee24e02-1f78-5b25-8d1c-f19b4a0052ee" :step/math-academy-id :tutorial/content "Given the matrix $[\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{B}|\mathcal{C}}$ of a linear map $\mathbf{T}:V \to W$ relative to the bases $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C},$ and the coordinates $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ of a vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to $\mathcal{B},$ the image of $\mathbf{x}$ under $\mathbf{T}$ with respect to the basis $\mathcal{C}$ can be found as 

$$
[\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{x})]_{\mathcal{C}} = 
[\mathbf{T}]_{{\mathcal{B}}|{\mathcal{C}}}\cdot [\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}
$$

For example, if

![](images/e3/e3623ffb88602004ad3ab01f55976d3a55759563a6088f4e2a10b7b8849a6f70.svg)

then the image of $\mathbf x$ under $\mathbf T$ relative to $\mathcal C$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}[T(x)]_{C} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -2 \\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "db73b6f4-55d4-5d30-856e-463bc6cc9964" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5093 :tutorial/title "The Image of a Vector Under a Linear Map Given by a Matrix Relative to Two Bases"} :step/id #uuid "14e61c95-f43b-5c3d-8e38-75c4db0838d1" :step/math-academy-id 31944 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125441}}] :activity/title "The Matrix of a Linear Map Relative to Two Bases" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186124752} {:db/id 17592186125440 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125799 :tutorial/content "Let's suppose we have the linear map

$$
\mathbf T: {\color{blue}V} \to {\color{red}W}
$$

where the bases of the vector spaces $\color{blue}V$ and ${\color{red}W}$ respectively are given by

$$
{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}=\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{b}_1},{\color{blue}\mathbf{b}_2}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{b}_3} \}, \qquad \qquad {\color{red}\mathcal{C}} = \{ {\color{red}\mathbf{c}_1},{\color{red}\mathbf{c}_2} \}.
$$

The **matrix of $\mathbf{T}$ with respect to the bases $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ and $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$** is the matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors $\mathbf{T}({\color{blue}\mathbf{b}_1}),$ $\mathbf{T}(\color{blue}{\mathbf{b}_2}),$ and $\mathbf{T}({\color{blue}\mathbf{b}_3})$ relative to the basis ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{B|C} & =[\begin{aligned}| & | & | \\ [T({b}_{1})]_{C} & [T({b}_{2})]_{C} & [T({b}_{3})]_{C} \\ | & | & |\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

For example, if 

![](images/be/be8cff88ef83ebc67d0df7a50a243c55c8f11aa92e7a07f64b73bb30ed701392.svg)

then

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{B|C} & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 10 & -12 \\ 1 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "da91373e-0973-56a4-91c9-aa2a2b1de0b1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3589 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "9ee24e02-1f78-5b25-8d1c-f19b4a0052ee" :step/math-academy-id 20152 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125546}} {:db/id 17592186125799 :tutorial/content "Let's suppose we have the linear map

operation to any $3\times 3$ matrix is the same as *pre-multiplying* (multiplying on the left) the matrix by the corresponding elementary matrix.

For instance, if we wish to swap the first row and the second row of a $3\times 3$ matrix $A,$ we pre-multiply $A$ by the corresponding elementary matrix 
![](images/2d/2de2ee02cbd3b00b6945fc8df8d84e83920fc0889c76394c1c726c94d68b1d99.svg)
to get $E_1 A.$

To perform a sequence of row operations to a $3\times 3$ matrix, we pre-multiply the matrix by the elementary matrix corresponding to the first operation, and then pre-multiply the result by the elementary matrix corresponding to the second operation.

For instance, given a $3 \times 3$ matrix $A,$ suppose that we would like to multiply the second row by $2$ and then add $3$ times the first row to the second row. To do this, we first pre-multiply $A$ by 
![](images/61/61f42ffa5ee0defeb3330421ead9c42f84200b274577c96cffe1d59ed9cf5cef.svg)
to get $E_2 A.$ Then we pre-multiply the result by 
![](images/be/be5d3785649ca7ac1557b43ca434c2558af417d29db47c10ef2938c1099db6f5.svg) 
to get $E_3 E_2 A.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c110a2ca-8856-5b26-9ded-2e9f35023747" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3171 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "fa6e7f35-addb-57cf-a360-9e6406254399" :step/content {:db/id 17592186069943 :tutorial/content "The **product rule for radicals** states that the square root of a product equals the product of the square roots:

$$
\begin{aligned} \sqrt{ab} &=\sqrt{a} \cdot \sqrt{b} \end{aligned}
$$

We can use the product rule to rewrite the square roots of algebraic expressions.

As an example, let's suppose we want to simplify the following expression:

$$
\sqrt{32y}
$$

First, we rewrite $32y$ as the product $16 \cdot 2y$, which contains a perfect square $(16){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned} \sqrt{32y} \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{16 \cdot 2y} \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{4^2 \cdot 2y}& \end{aligned}
$$

Then, we separate the product into two separate radicals using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned} \sqrt{4^2\cdot 2y} \\[3pt] &= \sqrt{4^2}\cdot \sqrt{2y}& \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify the radical containing the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned} \sqrt{4^2}\cdot \sqrt{2y} \\[3pt] &= \mid 4 \mid \cdot \sqrt{2y} \\[3pt] &= 4\sqrt{2y}& \end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "169256a7-1898-59b1-a7a9-f8cb8b713d51" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1606 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "bfc154dc-32b4-5e94-a701-30a255009a40" :step/math-academy-id 4304 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069764}} {:db/id 17592186069801 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068852 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068469 :question/id #uuid "969be012-a830-564e-a355-00a4f1985ae8" :question/math-academy-id "e-1363"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4df00200-f680-53f3-9b49-700b9ac14204" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050890}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069224} {:db/id 17592186069225}] :knowledge-point/title "Simplifying a Radical Expression That Is Not a Perfect Square With Domain Restrictions"} :step/id #uuid "16267a67-a93b-562b-88e6-0963346b1bfb" :step/math-academy-id 4311}] :activity/title "Simplifying Square Root Expressions Using the Product Rule" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186068936} {:db/id 17592186069800 :step/content {:db/id 17592186069943 :tutorial/content "The **product rule for radicals** states that the square root of a product equals the product of the square roots:

:step/math-academy-id 37757 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069762}} {:db/id 17592186069943 :tutorial/content "The **product rule for radicals** states that the square root of a product equals the product of the square roots:

$$
\begin{aligned} \sqrt{ab} &=\sqrt{a} \cdot \sqrt{b} \end{aligned}
$$

We can use the product rule to rewrite the square roots of algebraic expressions.

As an example, let's suppose we want to simplify the following expression:

$$
\sqrt{32y}
$$

First, we rewrite $32y$ as the product $16 \cdot 2y$, which contains a perfect square $(16){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned} \sqrt{32y} \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{16 \cdot 2y} \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{4^2 \cdot 2y}& \end{aligned}
$$

Then, we separate the product into two separate radicals using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned} \sqrt{4^2\cdot 2y} \\[3pt] &= \sqrt{4^2}\cdot \sqrt{2y}& \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify the radical containing the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned} \sqrt{4^2}\cdot \sqrt{2y} \\[3pt] &= \mid 4 \mid \cdot \sqrt{2y} \\[3pt] &= 4\sqrt{2y}& \end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "169256a7-1898-59b1-a7a9-f8cb8b713d51" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1606 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186050750 :topic/difficulty 1.1594003508920947 :topic/id #uuid the probability density function

$$

find the cumulative distribution function $F(x).$" :question/worked-solution "The cumulative distribution function of a continuous random variable $X$ is the function $F(x)$ defined by

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)={\int }_{-\infty }^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

For the given probability density function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{2{e}^{t}}{(1+{e}^{t})^{3}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={-\frac{1}{(1+{e}^{t})^{2}}|}_{-\infty }^{x} \\  & =-\frac{1}{(1+{e}^{x})^{2}}+1 \\  & =1-\frac{1}{(1+{e}^{x})^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186419956 :question/id #uuid "dbdaccde-7824-5d29-93f1-f05b495a99f8" :question/math-academy-id "q-126213"} {:db/id 17592186419958 :question/id #uuid "fb64e84b-4036-56ed-b5be-3b99c498406f" :question/math-academy-id "q-210762"} {:db/id 17592186424886 :question/id #uuid "2b70eaac-0c45-5da5-8a2f-2002d9071035" :question/math-academy-id "q-89727" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "492f777b-8264-55ab-9be1-d1359bd9513d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}" :db/id 17592186424871} {:answer/id #uuid "4a7a5540-6762-5260-9b7f-2a98061bf95e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{4}" :db/id 17592186424872} {:answer/id #uuid "50e4b7f0-64ef-587b-bfde-a4520b836560" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1+\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}" :db/id 17592186424873} {:answer/id #uuid "d60102cb-368c-5209-b3c3-06d9c44b89a2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}" :db/id 17592186424880} {:answer/id #uuid "ef55c585-a616-50c9-9382-ffb7b5a8ceda" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}" :db/id 17592186424881}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186424881} :answer-field/id #uuid "ce55fccd-c2b9-544b-881d-b59a7e7c0f42" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186424884}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)=\frac{{e}^{-|x/3|}}{6},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

its cumulative distribution function is 

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}^{x/3}}{2},\, & x<0 \\ h(x),\, & x\ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the function $h(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Since our random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that involves an absolute value, the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\{\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t, & x<0 \\ {\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t, & x\ge 0\end{aligned}
$$

Let's compute the integrals.

- If $x\le 0,$ we have

$$

Find the function $h(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Since our random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that is strictly positive only for $1\le x\le 4,$ the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<1 \\ {\int }_{1}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t, & 1\le x\le 4 \\ 1, & x>4\end{aligned}
$$

For the given probability density function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{1}^{x}-\frac{2}{9}(t-1)(t-4)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{x}-\frac{2}{9}({t}^{2}-5t+4)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={(-\frac{2}{27}{t}^{3}+\frac{5}{9}{t}^{2}-\frac{8}{9}t)|}_{1}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{2}{27}{x}^{3}+\frac{5}{9}{x}^{2}-\frac{8}{9}x-(-\frac{2}{27}+\frac{5}{9}-\frac{8}{9}) \\  & =-\frac{2}{27}{x}^{3}+\frac{5}{9}{x}^{2}-\frac{8}{9}x+\frac{11}{27}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<1 \\ -\frac{2}{27}{x}^{3}+\frac{5}{9}{x}^{2}-\frac{8}{9}x+\frac{11}{27}, & 1\le x\le 4 \\ 1, & x>4.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186442324 :question/id #uuid "990f1bb6-e595-59df-8c02-d323344bc3ca" :question/math-academy-id "q-210785" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "da4529e7-604e-506b-adaa-ff85312c20f9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{-x^{2}+8x-7}{9}" :db/id 17592186442316}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186442316} :answer-field/id #uuid "45ff772f-b783-5f66-89ac-69df3d1d8f2a" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186442319}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

:topic/math-academy-id 2163} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186134578 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135186 :tutorial/content "The cumulative distribution function (or CDF) of a continuous random variable is defined the same way as for a discrete random variable. 

Given a continuous random variable $X,$ the CDF is the function $F(x)$ such that

$$
F(x) = P(X \leq x).
$$

If our random variable has the probability density function (or PDF) $f(x),$ then we have

$$
F(x) = P(X \leq x) = \int_{-\infty}^x f(t) \, \textrm dt.
$$

Note that we use $f(t)dt$ in the integrand because $x$ serves as the upper limit of integration. 

For example, consider the random variable $X$ with the following PDF:

![](images/e7/e79c230f2b548c9280425f555f6d99a8f997e989289a05fb5f4584b656c4dcc8.svg)

Since $f(x)= 0$ for all $x < 0,$  we have

$$
F(x)  = \int_{-\infty}^x 0 \, \textrm dt = 0
$$

if $x<0.$

To compute the CDF for $x\geq 0,$  we integrate $f(x)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =0+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{2}{\pi (1+{t}^{2})}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\frac{2}{\pi }\operatorname{arctan}⁡t|}_{0}^{x} \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }\operatorname{arctan}⁡x-\frac{2}{\pi }(0) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing our CDF as a function defined over the entire real line, we get

![](images/66/66b7bf54271075ae72fcf07fa4dc8573a94e97c2b2cc77680c0ec94b6053f360.svg)" :tutorial/id #uuid "de1bbdf6-687d-537a-a6fe-03d9fafbe841" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8364 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "3f773be7-dfa4-524f-aec7-8ade124c5cea" :step/math-academy-id 132590 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134579}} {:db/id 17592186134579 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133726 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133516 :question/id #uuid "38b4473a-f956-5af5-863b-387dc10b4924" :question/math-academy-id "e-13362"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1d7509fa-a254-5b78-b307-3e0c4ef4d9ec" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049638}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134158} {:db/id 17592186134538} {:db/id 17592186419947} {:db/id 17592186419952} {:db/id 17592186419953} {:db/id 17592186424144} {:db/id 17592186424145}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a CDF Given a PDF With a Lower Bound"} :step/id #uuid "2411aa47-0b30-5e9c-b541-4d44b5f7aeed" :step/math-academy-id 132591 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134580}} {:db/id 17592186134580 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133727 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133517 :question/id #uuid "98dd834c-ac74-5cdd-88ee-060fd9ac689d" :question/math-academy-id "e-13363"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7b0ce833-e045-5aff-94a4-f9ad56cdb904" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134159} {:db/id 17592186134541} {:db/id 17592186419950} {:db/id 17592186419951} {:db/id 17592186419956} {:db/id 17592186419958} {:db/id 17592186424886} {:db/id 17592186442323}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing a CDF Given a PDF That’s Nonzero Over All Real Numbers"} :step/id #uuid "f242a3a5-626f-54b6-b0cc-b8af4506a3f0" :step/math-academy-id 132594 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134581}} {:db/id 17592186134581 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135187 :tutorial/content "When a random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that is strictly positive on the interval $a \leq x \leq b$ only, we have

- $P(X \leq x) = 0$ for $x < a,$ and

- $P(X \leq x) = 1$ for $x > b.$

In these cases, the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

![](images/7a/7a64bac7c252a3f52fc92f6364edb5c66f31e47da28e78eeb0d069d894135700.svg)" :tutorial/id #uuid "0794419f-6b72-568b-a787-d71121c8bcd9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8365 :tutorial/title "Finding a CDF Given a PDF With Lower and Upper Bounds"} :step/id #uuid "a74ce991-870f-5bfa-8a96-8bbed06ce5b6" :step/math-academy-id 132597 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134582}} {:db/id 17592186134582 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133728 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133518 :question/id #uuid "4159a407-ea9f-5728-b219-bf1afab732a2" :question/math-academy-id "e-13364"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "eedcfa3d-b02b-5f96-99f4-cd0a452d272a" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134150} {:db/id 17592186134160} {:db/id 17592186419943} {:db/id 17592186419949} {:db/id 17592186419954} {:db/id 17592186419955} {:db/id 17592186424143} {:db/id 17592186424888} {:db/id 17592186442324} {:db/id 17592186442325} {:db/id 17592186500304}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a CDF Given a PDF With Lower and Upper Bounds"} :step/id #uuid "47bc1334-f06b-5cc0-b191-427d1d862db4" :step/math-academy-id 132598 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134583}} {:db/id 17592186134583 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135188 :tutorial/content "As with discrete random variables, we can use the CDF of a continuous random variable to quickly compute a probability over an interval:

$$
P(a \leq X \leq b) = F(b) - F(a)
$$

For example, suppose that a random variable $X$ has the following CDF:

$$
F(x) = \dfrac{1}{1+e^{-x}}, \qquad -\infty < x < \infty.
$$

We can use the above CDF to quickly compute $P(0 \leq x \leq 1),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0\le x\le 1) & =F(1)-F(0) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{e}^{-1}}-\frac{1}{1+{e}^{0}} \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{e}^{-1}}-\frac{1}{2} \\  & ≈0.231\end{aligned}
$$

Remember that for continuous random variables, it doesn't matter whether or not we include the endpoints of the interval, so we have

$$
P(0 \leq X \leq 1) = P(0 < X \leq 1) = P(0 \leq X < 1) = P(0 < X < 1) = 0.231.
$$

In general, for a continuous random variable $X,$ we have

$$
P(a \leq X \leq b) = P(a < X \leq b) = P(a \leq X < b) = P(a < X < b) = F(b) - F(a).

Given a continuous random variable $X,$ the CDF is the function $F(x)$ such that

$$
F(x) = P(X \leq x).
$$

If our random variable has the probability density function (or PDF) $f(x),$ then we have

$$
F(x) = P(X \leq x) = \int_{-\infty}^x f(t) \, \textrm dt.
$$

Note that we use $f(t)dt$ in the integrand because $x$ serves as the upper limit of integration. 

For example, consider the random variable $X$ with the following PDF:

![](images/e7/e79c230f2b548c9280425f555f6d99a8f997e989289a05fb5f4584b656c4dcc8.svg)

Since $f(x)= 0$ for all $x < 0,$  we have

$$
F(x)  = \int_{-\infty}^x 0 \, \textrm dt = 0
$$

if $x<0.$

To compute the CDF for $x\geq 0,$  we integrate $f(x)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =0+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{2}{\pi (1+{t}^{2})}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\frac{2}{\pi }\operatorname{arctan}⁡t|}_{0}^{x} \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }\operatorname{arctan}⁡x-\frac{2}{\pi }(0) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing our CDF as a function defined over the entire real line, we get

$$
P(a \leq X \leq b) = F(b) - F(a)
$$

For example, suppose that a random variable $X$ has the following CDF:

$$
F(x) = \dfrac{1}{1+e^{-x}}, \qquad -\infty < x < \infty.
$$

We can use the above CDF to quickly compute $P(0 \leq x \leq 1),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0\le x\le 1) & =F(1)-F(0) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{e}^{-1}}-\frac{1}{1+{e}^{0}} \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{e}^{-1}}-\frac{1}{2} \\  & ≈0.231\end{aligned}
$$

Remember that for continuous random variables, it doesn't matter whether or not we include the endpoints of the interval, so we have

$$
P(0 \leq X \leq 1) = P(0 < X \leq 1) = P(0 \leq X < 1) = P(0 < X < 1) = 0.231.
$$

In general, for a continuous random variable $X,$ we have

$$
P(a \leq X \leq b) = P(a < X \leq b) = P(a \leq X < b) = P(a < X < b) = F(b) - F(a).
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e5203710-822b-55d4-9dfb-985bc4d41d6a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8366 :tutorial/title "Using a CDF to Compute a Probability Over an Interval"} :step/id #uuid "55418ca8-74f9-5755-9f75-2d411c4a476e" :step/math-academy-id 132601 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134584}} {:db/id 17592186135188 :tutorial/content "As with discrete random variables, we can use the CDF of a continuous random variable to quickly compute a probability over an interval:

$$
P(a \leq X \leq b) = F(b) - F(a)
$$

For example, suppose that a random variable $X$ has the following CDF:

$$
F(x) = \dfrac{1}{1+e^{-x}}, \qquad -\infty < x < \infty.
$$

We can use the above CDF to quickly compute $P(0 \leq x \leq 1),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0\le x\le 1) & =F(1)-F(0) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{e}^{-1}}-\frac{1}{1+{e}^{0}} \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{e}^{-1}}-\frac{1}{2} \\  & ≈0.231\end{aligned}
$$

Remember that for continuous random variables, it doesn't matter whether or not we include the endpoints of the interval, so we have

$$
P(0 \leq X \leq 1) = P(0 < X \leq 1) = P(0 \leq X < 1) = P(0 < X < 1) = 0.231.
$$

In general, for a continuous random variable $X,$ we have

$$
P(a \leq X \leq b) = P(a < X \leq b) = P(a \leq X < b) = P(a < X < b) = F(b) - F(a).
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e5203710-822b-55d4-9dfb-985bc4d41d6a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8366 :tutorial/title "Using a CDF to Compute a Probability Over an Interval"} {:db/id 17592186134584 "q-89727" :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)=\frac{{e}^{-|x/3|}}{6},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

its cumulative distribution function is 

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}^{x/3}}{2},\, & x<0 \\ h(x),\, & x\ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the function $h(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Since our random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that involves an absolute value, the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\{\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t, & x<0 \\ {\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t, & x\ge 0\end{aligned}
$$

Let's compute the integrals.

- If $x\le 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{2}|}_{-\infty }^{x} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{x/3}}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{x/3}}{2}|}_{x=0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & =-{\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{2}|}_{0}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}+(-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =1-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}^{x/3}}{2}, & x<0 \\ 1-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}, & x\ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3f2429d9-8a43-540c-8ee1-21b8c07473a4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186424890}} {:db/id 17592186424890 :step/content {:db/id 17592186424888 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "27f33f1e-6e04-5ef0-8a18-a9a9635e495a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{27}{x}^{3}+\frac{5}{9}{x}^{2}-\frac{8}{9}x+\frac{11}{27}" :db/id 17592186424869} {:answer/id #uuid "7bc40166-55c4-53b3-bf06-562cddc8e868" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{2}{27}{x}^{3}+\frac{5}{9}{x}^{2}-\frac{8}{9}x+\frac{11}{27}" :db/id 17592186424875} {:answer/id #uuid "8a0df617-e565-5181-bd27-09321bb7abfd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{2}{27}{x}^{3}+\frac{5}{9}{x}^{2}-\frac{8}{9}x+\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186424877} {:answer/id #uuid "a3e9b386-cf97-5734-82c8-f8b9318ea865" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{27}{x}^{3}+\frac{5}{9}{x}^{2}-\frac{8}{9}x+\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186424878} {:answer/id #uuid "fbbc1dbf-3cbe-5835-99b1-f9050b0ed224" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{27}{x}^{3}-\frac{5}{9}{x}^{2}+\frac{8}{9}x+\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186424882}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186424875} :answer-field/id #uuid "5340e926-2580-5f2f-bf08-46d25e342346" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186424883}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "97c91681-ff70-5452-bbfe-e1a92bb2e9d1" :question/math-academy-id "q-126156" :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{9}(x-1)(x-4),\, & 1\le x\le 4 \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

its cumulative distribution function is 

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0,\, & x<1 \\ h(x),\, & 1\le x\le 4 \\ 1,\, & x>4.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the function $h(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Since our random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that is strictly positive only for $1\le x\le 4,$ the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<1 \\ {\int }_{1}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t, & 1\le x\le 4 \\ 1, & x>4\end{aligned}
$$

For the given probability density function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{1}^{x}-\frac{2}{9}(t-1)(t-4)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{x}-\frac{2}{9}({t}^{2}-5t+4)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={(-\frac{2}{27}{t}^{3}+\frac{5}{9}{t}^{2}-\frac{8}{9}t)|}_{1}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{2}{27}{x}^{3}+\frac{5}{9}{x}^{2}-\frac{8}{9}x-(-\frac{2}{27}+\frac{5}{9}-\frac{8}{9}) \\  & =-\frac{2}{27}{x}^{3}+\frac{5}{9}{x}^{2}-\frac{8}{9}x+\frac{11}{27}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<1 \\ -\frac{2}{27}{x}^{3}+\frac{5}{9}{x}^{2}-\frac{8}{9}x+\frac{11}{27}, & 1\le x\le 4 \\ 1, & x>4.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "9bf4404a-eca3-5f58-9aa8-59a46fdb29aa"} {:db/id 17592186424891 :step/content {:db/id 17592186424887 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0d43dadc-2415-595b-83bd-07293e62a4d7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{5}" :db/id 17592186424868} {:answer/id #uuid "2d728c61-ee7a-5242-b976-dff68318b24a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{5}" :db/id 17592186424870} {:answer/id #uuid "54302da3-4ffd-5ae6-9474-e5f95bb705f9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186424874} {:answer/id #uuid "86635ef4-b567-5842-a8be-7564b4bc47cb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}" :db/id 17592186424876} {:answer/id #uuid "c53339f9-decf-5456-b59e-339275bad539" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{5}" :db/id 17592186424879}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186424870} :answer-field/id #uuid "cf2e7998-6dc3-5838-ae14-0d427c2b4449" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186424885}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "5d72a8e6-eda0-59be-829b-e0298d5412e1" :question/math-academy-id "q-89695" :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X$ has the cumulative distribution function

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<1 \\ 1-\frac{1}{x}, & x\ge 1,\end{aligned}
$$

find $P(X\le 5).$" :question/worked-solution "The cumulative distribution function of a continuous random variable $X$ is the function $F(x)$ defined by

$$

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\{\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t, & x<0 \\ {\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t, & x\ge 0\end{aligned}
$$

Let's compute the integrals.

- If $x\le 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{2}|}_{-\infty }^{x} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{x/3}}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{x/3}}{2}|}_{x=0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & =-{\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{2}|}_{0}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}+(-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =1-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}^{x/3}}{2}, & x<0 \\ 1-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}, & x\ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3f2429d9-8a43-540c-8ee1-21b8c07473a4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186424890}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "492f777b-8264-55ab-9be1-d1359bd9513d" :answer/type {:db/id $$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{64}x(16-{x}^{2}),\, & 0\le x\le 4 \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

its cumulative distribution function is 

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0,\, & x<0 \\ h(x),\, & 0\le x\le 4 \\ 1,\, & x>4.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the function $h(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Since our random variable $X$ has a probability density function $f(x)$ that is strictly positive only for $0<x<4,$ the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<0 \\ {\int }_{0}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t, & 0\le x\le 4 \\ 1, & x>4\end{aligned}
$$

For the given probability density function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{1}{64}t(16-{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\frac{1}{64}(8{t}^{2}-\frac{{t}^{4}}{4})|}_{0}^{x} \\  & =\frac{1}{64}(8{x}^{2}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{256}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

:question/math-academy-id "q-89672" :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}2(-x+4),\, & 3\le x\le 4 \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

its cumulative distribution function is 

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0,\, & x<3 \\ h(x),\, & 3\le x\le 4 \\ 1,\, & x>4.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the function $h(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Since our random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that is strictly positive only for $3\le x\le 4,$ the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<3 \\ {\int }_{3}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t, & 3\le x\le 4 \\ 1, & x>4\end{aligned}
$$

For the given probability density function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{3}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{3}^{x}2(-t+4)\,\text{d}t \\ \text{ } & ={8t-{t}^{2}|}_{3}^{x} \\  & =-{x}^{2}+8x-15.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<3 \\ -{x}^{2}+8x-15, & 3\le x\le 4 \\ 1, & x>4.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "4853d037-9366-5cfe-b2a6-ea749a958948" :step/next {:db/id 17592186500408}} {:db/id 17592186500402 :step/content {:db/id 17592186500293 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0e338a7c-f5c5-55b6-800b-47f10296b1d7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{112}{729}" :db/id 17592186499686} {:answer/id #uuid "4673f4bc-028d-52bd-b6cb-43a313197f90" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{23}{1458}" :db/id 17592186499785} {:answer/id #uuid "60d5eb82-e934-5a50-abfb-6bb988e212e5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{230}{729}" :db/id 17592186499844} {:answer/id #uuid "aa8b3642-18a5-59b9-ba90-c44b1dc2ff93" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{130}{729}" :db/id 17592186499989} {:answer/id #uuid "b05849a6-fd14-5761-ac6a-f3df6f46c897" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{113}{1458}" :db/id 17592186500007}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186499844} :answer-field/id #uuid "ecc71117-bad7-5cf6-bbde-8b45ac8873de" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186500274}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "2175ed2b-85f5-5f4e-9b21-fd44965b957e" :question/math-academy-id "q-126173" :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X$ has the cumulative distribution function

$$
f(x)=\frac{{e}^{-|x/3|}}{6},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

its cumulative distribution function is 

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}^{x/3}}{2},\, & x<0 \\ h(x),\, & x\ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the function $h(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Since our random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that involves an absolute value, the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\{\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t, & x<0 \\ {\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t, & x\ge 0\end{aligned}
$$

Let's compute the integrals.

- If $x\le 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{2}|}_{-\infty }^{x} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{x/3}}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{x/3}}{2}|}_{x=0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & =-{\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{2}|}_{0}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}+(-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =1-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}^{x/3}}{2}, & x<0 \\ 1-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}, & x\ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "62b3bf85-d97a-532c-9a1f-d9d9bafa37cd" :step/next {:db/id 17592186500402}} {:db/id 17592186500442 :step/content {:db/id 17592186442324 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "da4529e7-604e-506b-adaa-ff85312c20f9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{-x^{2}+8x-7}{9}" :db/id 17592186442316}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186442316} :answer-field/id #uuid "45ff772f-b783-5f66-89ac-69df3d1d8f2a" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186442319}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "990f1bb6-e595-59df-8c02-d323344bc3ca" :question/math-academy-id "q-210785" :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

"q-89727" :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)=\frac{{e}^{-|x/3|}}{6},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

its cumulative distribution function is 

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}^{x/3}}{2},\, & x<0 \\ h(x),\, & x\ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the function $h(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Since our random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that involves an absolute value, the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\{\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t, & x<0 \\ {\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t, & x\ge 0\end{aligned}
$$

Let's compute the integrals.

- If $x\le 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{2}|}_{-\infty }^{x} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{x/3}}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{x/3}}{2}|}_{x=0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & =-{\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{2}|}_{0}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}+(-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =1-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}^{x/3}}{2}, & x<0 \\ 1-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}, & x\ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "62b3bf85-d97a-532c-9a1f-d9d9bafa37cd" :step/next {:db/id 17592186500402}} {:db/id 17592186500402 :step/content {:db/id 17592186500293 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0e338a7c-f5c5-55b6-800b-47f10296b1d7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{112}{729}" :db/id 17592186499686} {:answer/id #uuid "4673f4bc-028d-52bd-b6cb-43a313197f90" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{23}{1458}" :db/id 17592186499785} {:answer/id #uuid "60d5eb82-e934-5a50-abfb-6bb988e212e5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{230}{729}" :db/id 17592186499844} {:answer/id #uuid "aa8b3642-18a5-59b9-ba90-c44b1dc2ff93" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{130}{729}" :db/id 17592186499989} {:answer/id #uuid "b05849a6-fd14-5761-ac6a-f3df6f46c897" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{113}{1458}" :db/id 17592186500007}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186499844} :answer-field/id #uuid "ecc71117-bad7-5cf6-bbde-8b45ac8873de" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186500274}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "2175ed2b-85f5-5f4e-9b21-fd44965b957e" :question/math-academy-id "q-126173" :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X$ has the cumulative distribution function

What is the general solution of the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)?$" :question/worked-solution "Given a system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),
$$

where $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1},{\lambda }_{2}$ with corresponding eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2},$ the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, the general solution of our matrix differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186348258 :question/id #uuid "6bfac1d8-b297-5aeb-80ab-63193055e75b" :question/math-academy-id "q-79672"} {:db/id 17592186348259 :question/id #uuid The population has nails of two different lengths, $5\,\text{cm}$ and $\text{10}\,\text{cm},$ distributed in the ratio $4:1.$ Calculate the standard error of $\overset{―}{X}.$ Round your answer to two decimal places." :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "If ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population variance ${\sigma }^{2},$ then

$$
\text{E}[\overset{―}{X}]=\mu ,\,\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n},
$$

and the standard error is given by

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]}=\frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

We're told that the nails in the population have lengths $5\,\text{cm}$ and $\text{10}\,\text{cm},$ and these are distributed in the ratio $4:1.$ Therefore, to compute the population mean and variance, we can consider a population consisting of $4+1=5$ nails only with the following lengths:

$$
5\,\text{cm},\,5\,\text{cm},\,5\,\text{cm},\,5\,\text{cm}\,10\,\text{cm}.
$$

Therefore, the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\frac{1}{5}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(4\cdot 5+10) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(20+10) \\  & =\frac{30}{5} \\  & =6\,\text{cm},\end{aligned}
$$

and the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\frac{1}{5}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i}^{2}-{\mu }^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(4\cdot {5}^{2}+{10}^{2})-{6}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(200)-36 \\  & =40-36 \\  & =4\,{\text{cm}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the sample size $n=3,$ we have

$$
\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}=\frac{4}{3}\,{\text{cm}}^{2}.
$$

Finally,

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\frac{4}{3}}≈1.15\,\text{cm}
$$

$$
\text{E}[\overset{―}{X}]=\mu ,\,\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n},
$$

and the standard error is given by

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]}=\frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

We're told that the employees in the population have working hours $38\,\text{h/week}$ and $40\,\text{h/week},$ and these are distributed in the ratio $3:1.$ Therefore, to compute the population's mean and variance, we can consider a population consisting of $3+1=4$ employees only with the following working hours:

$$
38\,\text{h/week},\,38\,\text{h/week},\,38\,\text{h/week},\,40\,\text{h/week}.
$$

Therefore, the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\frac{1}{4}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(3\cdot 38+40) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(114+40) \\  & =\frac{154}{4} \\  & =38.5\,\text{h/week},\end{aligned}
$$

and the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\frac{1}{4}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i}^{2}-{\mu }^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(3\cdot {38}^{2}+{40}^{2})-{38.5}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(5\,932)-1\,482.25 \\  & =1\,483-1\,482.25 \\  & =0.75\,{(\text{h/week})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the population standard deviation is $\sigma =\sqrt{0.75},$ and we have that 

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\frac{0.75}{n}}.
$$

We require that the standard error is less than $0.5\,\text{h/week}.$ Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{0.75}{n}} & <0.5 \\ \sqrt{n} & >\frac{\sqrt{0.75}}{0.5} \\ \sqrt{n} & >\sqrt{\frac{0.75}{{0.5}^{2}}} \\ \sqrt{n} & >\sqrt{\frac{0.75}{0.25}} \\ \sqrt{n} & >\sqrt{3} \\ n & >3.\end{aligned}
$$

:answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186413413}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the following joint probability density function:

$$
f(x,y)={\begin{aligned}24xy, & \,0<x<1,0<y<1-x \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Find $P(Y<X\,|\,X=\frac{1}{3}).$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that 

$$
P(Y\in A\,|\,X=x)={\int }_{A}{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y,
$$

where ${f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)$ is the conditional probability density function of $Y$ given $X=x.$ 

Using the formula for the marginal density function for $X,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1-x}24xy\,\text{d}y \\  & =24x{\int }_{0}^{1-x}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =24x{[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{1-x} \\  & =12x(1-x)^{2}-0 \\  & =12x(x-1)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the full expression for ${f}_{X}(x)$ is the following:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)={\begin{aligned}12x(x-1)^{2}, & \,0<x<1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Now recall that the conditional probability density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ for two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)}.
$$

where

- $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability density function for $X$ and $Y,$ and

- ${f}_{X}(x)$ is the marginal density function for $X.$

Now, for $0<x<1,0<y<1-x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{24xy}{12x(x-1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2y}{(x-1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

For other values of $x$ and $y,$ the function $f(x,y)$ equals $0.$ As a result, ${f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)$ will be equal to $0$ too.

Therefore, the conditional probability density function is the following:

$$
{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x)={\begin{aligned}\frac{2y}{(x-1)^{2}}, & \,0<x<1,0<y<1-x \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute our probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y<X\,|\,X=\frac{1}{3}) & =P(Y<\frac{1}{3}\,|\,X=\frac{1}{3}) \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/3}{f}_{Y\,|\,X}(y\,|\,x=\frac{1}{3})\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1/3}\frac{2y}{{(\frac{1}{3}-1)}^{2}}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1/3}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1/3} \\  & =\frac{9}{2}(\frac{1}{18}-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186411871 :question/id #uuid "dd343afe-c54e-593d-8dc2-ed57fc5e3a91" :question/math-academy-id "q-143625"} {:db/id 17592186413415 :question/id #uuid "6fd86b7a-aa64-5ea3-a90b-7af5da2353f8" :question/math-academy-id "q-143574" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0232ff5b-0d05-5778-88a0-ff0af66fc111" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{15}{16}" :db/id 17592186413397} {:answer/id #uuid "0d7ebaa8-7f99-5427-8a2f-237d9f6e4410" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{27}{64}" :db/id 17592186413398} {:answer/id #uuid "291ffaa1-af34-572c-8208-632d599387b4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{8}{9}" :db/id 17592186413399} {:answer/id #uuid "2bab8694-81fe-5f61-ab63-c2f3224466f2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{9}" :db/id 17592186413401} {:answer/id #uuid "cb999cce-827d-57cd-aed2-f09c922819e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{16}" :db/id 17592186413407}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186413398} :answer-field/id #uuid "76914fbd-7e46-5e1e-a2ea-82b62a7c5f3c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186413414}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the following joint probability density function:

$$
f(x,y)={\begin{aligned}8xy, & \,0\le x\le y,\,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Find $P(\frac{1}{4}<X<\frac{1}{2}\,|\,Y=\frac{2}{3}).$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that 

$$
P(Y\in A\,|\,X=x)={\int }_{A}{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}y,
$$

where ${f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)$ is the conditional probability density function of $X$ given $Y=y.$ 

Using the formula for the marginal density function for $Y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{y}8xy\,\text{d}x \\  & =8y{\int }_{0}^{y}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =8y{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{y} \\  & =4y({y}^{2}-0) \\  & =4{y}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the full expression for ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the following:

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)={\begin{aligned}4{y}^{3}, & \,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Now recall that the conditional probability density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ for two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)}.
$$

where

- $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability density function for $X$ and $Y,$ and

- ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the marginal density function for $Y.$

Now, for $0\le x\le 1,0\le y\le x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{8xy}{4{y}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2x}{{y}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

For other values of $x$ and $y,$ the function $f(x,y)$ equals $0.$ As a result, ${f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)$ will be equal to $0$ too.

Therefore, the conditional probability density function is the following:

$$
{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)={\begin{aligned}\frac{2x}{{y}^{2}}, & \,0\le x\le y,\,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute our probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\frac{1}{4}<X<\frac{1}{2}\,|\,Y=\frac{2}{3}) & ={\int }_{1/4}^{1/2}{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y=\frac{2}{3})\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1/4}^{1/2}\frac{2x}{{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{9}{4}{\int }_{1/4}^{1/2}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{9}{4}{[{x}^{2}]}_{1/4}^{1/2} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{16}) \\  & =\frac{9}{4}(\frac{3}{16}) \\  & =\frac{27}{64}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186162114 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161680 :question/id #uuid "f1c9e136-57b3-59ae-90e0-b28921be44ee" :question/math-academy-id "e-10101"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "eb3b4b6a-3a24-5079-bf33-ed1c5576ffa7" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186162390 :question/id #uuid "3d20c523-ad94-5c8f-adf5-6fe709391a09" :question/math-academy-id "q-143459"} {:db/id 17592186162396 :question/id #uuid "228badef-897c-5f4a-80d9-699c2c689782" :question/math-academy-id "q-143634"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Conditional PDF"} {:db/id 17592186161680 :question/id #uuid "f1c9e136-57b3-59ae-90e0-b28921be44ee" :question/math-academy-id "e-10101"} {:db/id 17592186162390 :question/id #uuid "3d20c523-ad94-5c8f-adf5-6fe709391a09" :question/math-academy-id "q-143459" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186162114 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "eb3b4b6a-3a24-5079-bf33-ed1c5576ffa7" :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Conditional PDF"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9baef0ad-50bb-5117-a90e-f69d88309a80" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2 - $$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{2y(2x+3y)}{5}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(\frac{4xy}{5}+\frac{6{y}^{2}}{5})\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{2{x}^{2}y}{5}+\frac{6x{y}^{2}}{5}]}_{x=1}^{x=2} \\  & =\frac{8y}{5}+\frac{12{y}^{2}}{5}-\frac{2y}{5}-\frac{6{y}^{2}}{5} \\  & =\frac{6{y}^{2}}{5}+\frac{6y}{5} \\  & =\frac{6y(y+1)}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the full expression for ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the following:

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)={\begin{aligned}\frac{6y(y+1)}{5}, & \,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Now recall that the conditional probability density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ for two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)},
$$

where

- $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability density function for $X$ and $Y,$ and

- ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the marginal density function for $Y.$

Now, for $1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2y(2x+3y)}{5})}{(\frac{6y(y+1)}{5})} \\  & =\frac{2x+3y}{3(y+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

For other values of $x$ and $y,$ the function $f(x,y)$ equals $0.$ As a result, ${f}_{X\,|\,Y}(x\,|\,y)$ will be equal to $0$ too.

$$

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "![](images/04/0457cb819e6f39ef9c0978e356cff788e1cf5edbef9cbf844a054ab777b70eac.png)

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a the line segment from the point $A(-2,0)$ to the point $B(0,1),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of the line segment from the point $B(0,1)$ to the point $D(1,1).$

Given that ${\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=-\frac{3}{2},$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(x-2y)\,i+(y-x)\,j,$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

We're given the value of the second integral, so we only need to work out the first.

The path ${C}_{1}$ is the line segment from $A$ to $B.$  It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =⟨-2,0⟩+t(⟨0,1⟩-⟨-2,0⟩) \\  & =⟨-2+2t,t⟩ \\  & =(-2+2t)i+t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<1.$ Along this segment, we have $x=-2+2t$ and $y=t.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t)) & =(x-2y)\,i+(y-x)\,j \\  & =((-2+2t)-2t)\,i+(t-(-2+2t))\,j \\  & =-2\,i+(2-t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2+2t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =2\,i+j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =(-2\,i+(2-t)\,j)\cdot (2\,i+j) \\  & =-2-t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t+(-\frac{3}{2}) \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-2-t)\,\text{d}t-\frac{3}{2} \\  & ={[-2t-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1}-\frac{3}{2} \\  & =[-2(1)-\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}-0]-\frac{3}{2} \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}-\frac{3}{2} \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186415770 :question/id #uuid "3412530f-81b3-51bb-95a9-4599a55eb207" :question/math-academy-id "q-77250"} {:db/id 17592186415774 :question/id #uuid "8399ab15-70cf-5db8-b1d1-61088de736be" :question/math-academy-id "q-77244"} {:db/id 17592186424621 :question/id #uuid "515517e3-98f2-5a9f-ba03-8d3b47263ffd" :question/math-academy-id "q-77258" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "23b97760-1703-5852-afc4-69acd21e7cc9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "32" :db/id 17592186424603} {:answer/id #uuid "4bd6afbc-8569-51f5-a569-dd388d648b11" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186424605} {:answer/id #uuid "79d50006-6f06-56c3-bce2-b65f3e1eb21c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186424607} {:answer/id #uuid "d37fe04f-4a91-5f51-9524-f7477c2a7f9a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186424612} {:answer/id #uuid "e17522ae-4622-53a9-bb60-7bec4bbcce91" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186424613}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186424605} :answer-field/id #uuid "7fdba31b-0f4f-583e-a52e-f0510ad8e3c8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186424617}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "![](images/4d/4d4c2c86ed8506ff034141ac20a5a56587a80370384ceeaf08c66f2ce3e8a315.png)

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a section of the parabola $y=-\sqrt{x}$ from the point $O(0,0)$ to the point $A(4,-2),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of a line segment from the point $A(4,-2)$ to the point $B(4,0).$

Given that ${\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=\frac{8}{3},$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=x\,i+{y}^{2}\,j$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

We're given the value of the second integral, so we only need to work out the first.

The path ${C}_{1}$ is the section of the curve $y=-\sqrt{x}$ from $O$ to $A.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}(t)=t\,i-\sqrt{t}\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 4.$ Along this curve, we have $x=t$ and $y=-\sqrt{t}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t)) & =x\,i+{y}^{2}\,j \\  & =t\,i+t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\sqrt{t})j \\  & =i-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =(t\,i+t\,j)\cdot (i-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}\,j) \\  & =t-\frac{\sqrt{t}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t+\frac{8}{3} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(t-\frac{\sqrt{t}}{2})\text{d}t+\frac{8}{3} \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{t}^{3/2}}{3}]}_{0}^{4}+\frac{8}{3} \\  & =(\frac{{4}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{4}^{3/2}}{3}-0)+\frac{8}{3} \\  & =\frac{16}{3}+\frac{8}{3} \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186179672 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179527 :question/id #uuid "2e6103cc-7be6-5eb6-ab5a-aa5aff3fa423" :question/math-academy-id "e-6319"} :knowledge-point/id "![](images/13/13e4c6a06a44099024ce91ef6c9ed4679af037c2e794351597a4d604bf39dc6f.png)

Consider the ellipse $E$ and vector field $F$ shown above. Let $C$ be any path where $E$ is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction. Which of the following statements are true?

I. ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0$

II. ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$

III. ${∮}_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0$" :question/worked-solution "The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

We now recall the following:

- If the force works *with* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force helps to push the particle along the path), then ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r>0.$

- If the force works *against* the motion of the particle (i.e., the force impedes the motion of the particle as it moves along the path), then ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r<0.$

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is true, while statement II is false. Since the force $F$ acts perpendicular to the motion of the particle as it moves around $C,$ it neither helps nor hinders its motion. 

![](images/63/6371bb04d33719ee18c65a92354e84be0e9077e780eac9559dcb7ec42deb8d99.png)

So, ${∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.$

- Statement III is false. If we reverse the orientation of $C,$ then the situation with regards to the work done by $F$ remains unchanged.

![](images/0b/0bd9476fa9b19f04b40fbb9cca2986ed90495aa134307606622ef91070af19a7.png)

So, ${∮}_{-C}F\cdot \text{d}r=0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""} {:db/id 17592186455485 :question/id #uuid "a9318e5b-e833-584c-92bb-558dab7e94de" :question/math-academy-id "q-125640" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "029ef420-9eaa-5c6d-8287-3ef33710e976" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186454907} {:answer/id #uuid "3af01276-3947-5c77-abb0-001b7f9268cb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186455000} {:answer/id #uuid "74a31f1c-47e3-545d-a815-1b80644ceb5a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186455118} {:answer/id #uuid "c134f711-db33-5b9e-bc96-94b44710886e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186455236} {:answer/id #uuid "ce1d9b86-ba57-557d-9af4-ca1029204f80" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186455261}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186455000} :answer-field/id #uuid "07b21c95-dc62-58a4-b763-c93eafdfda09" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186455342}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "![](images/a1/a1883ee3a3a99d43109bae2d2093aef35548dde9753cfb7dc19dfd77a104ec83.png)

$F(x,y)=\frac{1}{y}\,i+\frac{1}{x}\,j$ along the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ oriented counterclockwise." :question/worked-solution "The closed curve $C$ is the circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{y}\,i+\frac{1}{x}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i+\frac{1}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\frac{1}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,i+\frac{1}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\,j)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =\frac{1}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\frac{1}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-1+1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we conclude that:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186179743 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179605 :question/id #uuid "1e15ae93-0a63-506a-a0ae-b15e035f0494" :question/math-academy-id "e-9543"} :knowledge-point/id :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186278161}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v),$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=⟨2x+y,\,2z,\,y+z⟩,\,r(u,v)=⟨-{u}^{2},\,2{u}^{2}-{v}^{2},\,{v}^{2}⟩,\,(u,v)\in D⊂{R}^{2}.
$$

If the flux of $F$ across $S$ with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A
$$

what is the missing expression?

*Hint: You can use the fact that ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}=⟨8uv,\,4uv,\,4uv⟩.$*" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Notice we are told that the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}=⟨8uv,\,4uv,\,4uv⟩.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨2x+y,\,2z,\,y+z⟩{|}_{x=-{u}^{2}\,y=2{u}^{2}-{v}^{2}\,z={v}^{2}} \\  & =⟨2(-{u}^{2})+(2{u}^{2}-{v}^{2}),\,2({v}^{2}),\,(2{u}^{2}-{v}^{2})+{v}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-{v}^{2},\,2{v}^{2},\,2{u}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨-{v}^{2},\,2{v}^{2},\,2{u}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨8uv,\,4uv,\,4uv⟩ \\  & =(-{v}^{2})\cdot 8uv+2{v}^{2}\cdot 4uv+2{u}^{2}\cdot 4uv \\  & =-8u{v}^{3}+8u{v}^{3}+8{u}^{3}v \\  & =8{u}^{3}v.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,8{u}^{3}v\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186278446 :question/id #uuid "a99addda-c910-54da-a8cb-ae3a5ce916a4" :question/math-academy-id "q-161249"} {:db/id 17592186278470 :question/id #uuid :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v),$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=⟨z,\,xz,\,yz⟩,\,r(u,v)=⟨u,\,{u}^{2},\,v⟩,\,(u,v)\in D⊂{R}^{2}.
$$

If the flux of $F$ across $S$ with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}auv+b{u}^{2}v\,\text{d}A
$$

what is the value of $a+b?$" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}({u}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,2u,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}({u}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 2u & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}2u & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 2u \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨2u,\,-1,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨z,\,xz,\,yz⟩{|}_{x=u\,y={u}^{2}\,z=v} \\  & =⟨v,\,uv,\,{u}^{2}v⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨v,\,uv,\,{u}^{2}v⟩\cdot ⟨2u,\,-1,\,0⟩ \\  & =v\cdot 2u+uv\cdot (-1)+{u}^{2}v\cdot 0 \\  & =2uv-uv+0 \\  & =uv.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}1\cdot uv+0\cdot {u}^{2}v\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b=1+0=1.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198380 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198022 :question/id #uuid "0364a11f-e567-517e-acf2-471708dbdc0a" :question/math-academy-id "e-12358"} :knowledge-point/id "Evaluate the surface integral

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨x,\,y,\,-z⟩\cdot \text{d}S
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u+v,\,v-u,\,uv⟩
$$

over the domain $D=\{(u,v)\,:\,-2\le u\le 0,\,0\le v\le 1\}.$

*Hint: You can use the fact that ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}=⟨-u-v,\,v-u,\,2⟩.$*" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

We're given that the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}=⟨-u-v,\,v-u,\,2⟩.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & ={⟨x,\,y,\,-z⟩|}_{x=u+v\,y=v-u\,z=uv} \\  & =⟨u+v,\,v-u,\,-uv⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨u+v,\,v-u,\,-uv⟩\cdot ⟨-u-v,\,v-u,\,2⟩ \\  & =(u+v)\cdot (-u-v)+(v-u)\cdot (v-u)+(-uv)\cdot 2 \\  & =-{u}^{2}-2uv-{v}^{2}+{v}^{2}-2uv+{u}^{2}-2uv \\  & =-6uv\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral evaluates to

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨x,\,y,\,-z⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-6uv)\,\text{d}A \\  & =-6{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-2}^{0}uv\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =-6{\int }_{0}^{1}v\,\text{d}v{\int }_{-2}^{0}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-6\cdot [\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}]_{0}^{1}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{-2}^{0} \\  & =-6\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot (-2) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048253} {:db/id 17592186049333 :topic/difficulty 0.9374657830854888 :topic/id #uuid "ec9aa34d-69be-5e48-a2c9-562d23408d0d" :topic/knowledge-points [{:db/id 17592186198408 {:db/id 17592186199465 :tutorial/content "Recall that the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F$ across a smooth, orientable surface $S$ with respect to the unit normal vector $\mathbf{n}$ is given by 

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf F \cdot \textrm{d} \mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S  \mathbf F \cdot {\color{blue}\mathbf{n}} \,\textrm{d}S,
$$

where ${\color{blue}\mathbf{n}}$ is a unit normal vector that defines the orientation of the surface.

![](images/9a/9aa63a1e4f1d278cef6c53600e8fb9c60829de972ba7409afdc32837ecbc3e07.png)

If $S$ is given by a parametric equation of the form 

$$
\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{r}(u,v), \qquad (u,v)\in D\subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,
$$

we can determine the unit normal vector using the fundamental product as follows:

$$
{\color{blue}\mathbf{n}} = \dfrac{\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v}{\| \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \|}
$$

 

Substituting this into the formula for the flux, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot \frac{{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}}{‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot \frac{{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}}{‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖}\,‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if $S$ is a smooth, orientable surface given in parametric form by $\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,$ then the flux of the vector field $\mathbf{F}$ across $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf F \cdot \textrm{d} \mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_D  \mathbf F(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v) \: \textrm{d}A.
$$
